## How to look after a leather sofa — https://www.learntoupholster.com/blog/how-to-look-after-a-leather-sofa

### How do you care for a leather sofa?

Keep it out of direct sunlight and away from radiators, dust it weekly, wipe it occasionally with a barely damp cloth and dry it straight away, condition it once or twice a year with a product matched to its finish, and blot spills immediately rather than rubbing them. Never use baby wipes, household cleaning sprays, solvents, silicone polish or olive oil on it. Everything else depends on which finish you have — pigmented, semi-aniline or aniline — and a drop of water will tell you that in two minutes.

Leather is the easiest upholstery material to look after and the one most often ruined by people trying to look after it. Almost all of the damage I see was caused by cleaning rather than by use.

The good news is that the actual routine is very small. The important part is knowing what you are working with first.

### Find out what finish you have

This decides every other decision, and it takes two minutes. Find somewhere inconspicuous — the back, or under a cushion — and put a single drop of water on it.

- The drop sits on the surface as a bead. Pigmented — also called protected or corrected-grain. Much the most common upholstery leather. It has a pigment layer and a topcoat over it, so the colour is uniform, natural markings are hidden, and the surface feels smooth and slightly cool. It is the most robust and the easiest to look after.

- The drop soaks in within a few seconds and darkens the leather. Aniline — dyed right through with no protective coating. Natural scars and grain variation show. It feels warm and soft, it develops the best patina of any leather, and it stains if you look at it wrongly.

- The drop sits briefly, then slowly darkens. Semi-aniline — dyed through with a light protective coat. Middle ground in every sense.

- Velvety, matt, marks when you brush your hand across it. Nubuck or suede. Different material entirely. Never use liquid on it; it wants a specialist brush and a specialist cleaner.

Wipe the drop off afterwards either way. And if the surface is flaking or lifting anywhere, stop — you may not have leather at all, which is covered in why leather peels.

### The routine, which is smaller than you think

Weekly: dust it. That is genuinely most of the job. Household dust is abrasive, and on a surface that gets sat on it works like very fine sandpaper against the finish. A dry microfibre cloth is enough.

Monthly: vacuum the crevices and the cushion joins with a soft brush attachment. Never a hard nozzle straight onto the leather — the plastic edge scratches finishes.

Occasionally: wipe over with a cloth wrung out in clean water so it is barely damp, then dry immediately with a second cloth. Not wet. Not soaked. On aniline, be even more sparing, because water alone can leave a ring.

Twice a year, or once if the house is not heavily heated: condition it.

### Conditioning, and what it actually does

People talk about feeding leather as though it were hungry. What conditioners really do is replace the oils and plasticisers that keep the fibre structure flexible, and maintain the finish sitting on top. Leather that dries out loses flexibility, and leather that has lost flexibility cracks when it flexes — which it does every time somebody sits down.

Practical points:

- Match the product to the finish. A conditioner for pigmented leather is not the right thing for aniline, and an aniline product can darken or blotch a protected leather. Read the label, and if it does not say, do not buy it.

- Test on a hidden area first and leave it a few hours before doing the whole piece.

- Little and often beats a lot occasionally. A thin application, worked in with a soft cloth, excess buffed off. Leather cannot absorb a thick coat, so the surplus just sits there attracting dust.

- More often in a dry, heated house or if the sofa lives near a radiator. Central heating is what dries leather out, not use.

### The things that quietly destroy it

This list matters more than everything above, because these do damage that cannot be undone.

- Baby wipes. The great destroyer, and the one I see most. They contain surfactants and often alcohol, they strip the finish a little at a time, and people use them precisely because they seem gentle. By the time the surface starts looking patchy the finish has already gone.

- Household cleaning sprays and antibacterial wipes. Same problem, faster.

- Solvents, alcohol, nail polish remover, white spirit. Dissolve the finish on contact.

- Silicone furniture polish. Builds a layer that looks glossy and then cannot be removed, and a leather with silicone on it cannot be properly recoloured later. It closes the door on the repair you will eventually want.

- Olive oil and other kitchen remedies. They go rancid, they darken unevenly, and they never come out.

- Saddle soap. Made for unfinished tack leather, too harsh for finished upholstery leather.

- Direct sunlight. The single biggest cause of fading and drying, and entirely preventable. If you can see where the sun falls across the back cushions, move the sofa or close the curtains.

- Radiators and log burners. A sofa with one end against a heat source will age visibly faster at that end.

If you take one thing from this article: stop using baby wipes on leather. More sofas are ruined by them than by children, dogs and spills combined.

### Spills

Blot, never rub. Rubbing pushes liquid into the grain and, on aniline, spreads the stain outwards into a bigger and more visible ring.

- Water and most drinks: blot immediately with a dry cloth, then let it dry naturally away from heat. Do not aim a hairdryer at it.

- Grease, butter, food oils: blot, then sprinkle talc or cornflour over the mark and leave it several hours to draw the oil out. Brush off gently. Repeat rather than scrubbing.

- Ink: leave it alone and ring a specialist. Every home remedy for ink on leather — hairspray especially — works by dissolving the finish, which means you trade a small ink mark for a permanent bare patch.

- Pet accidents: blot, clean gently with a leather-appropriate cleaner, and get to it quickly. Urine damages leather chemically as well as leaving a smell.

### Two problems people do not expect

Denim dye transfer. Dark jeans on a pale sofa transfer indigo into the leather, particularly on aniline and semi-aniline where there is little or no protective coat. It builds up gradually and is very difficult to remove once it has been there a while. If you have a light-coloured leather, deal with it early and often rather than waiting.

Scratches. On aniline and semi-aniline, light scratches often disappear if you warm them with a fingertip and buff gently with a soft cloth — the leather is dyed through, so there is colour underneath. On pigmented leather a scratch that has gone through the finish shows a different colour underneath and will not buff out; that is a job for a leather refinisher, who can fill and recolour it.

### Habits that add years

- Rotate and turn loose cushions so wear spreads evenly.

- Do not sit on the arms — arms are the least supported part of the frame and the first leather to stretch.

- Keep pets' claws trimmed if they are on the sofa, which they are.

- Keep it a foot clear of walls and radiators so air circulates behind it.

### When to call somebody

Leather refinishing is a proper trade in its own right, and a good refinisher can clean back, fill, recolour and reseal a tired pigmented leather to a standard that surprises people. That is very often the right answer for a sofa that looks past it but has a sound frame — considerably cheaper than recovering, and it keeps the original leather.

If the leather itself has split or torn through, that becomes an upholstery job: panel replacement rather than refinishing.

### What good looks like

The last thing worth saying is that leather is meant to change. A hide that has softened, darkened slightly and taken on the shape of the people who use it is not damaged — that is the whole point of buying leather rather than something that stays identical until it fails.

Dust it, keep it out of the sun, condition it twice a year, and keep the baby wipes in the kitchen. That is the entire job, and it will still look good in twenty years.

### Common questions

#### How often should you condition a leather sofa?

Once or twice a year for most homes, more often if the house is dry or heavily heated, or if the sofa sits near a radiator. Use a conditioner matched to the finish — a pigmented-leather product on aniline, or the reverse, can darken or blotch it. Apply thinly, work it in with a soft cloth and buff off the excess, because leather cannot absorb a thick coat.

#### Can you use baby wipes on a leather sofa?

No. They are the most common cause of avoidable damage to leather upholstery. The surfactants, and often alcohol, strip the protective finish a small amount at a time, and by the point the surface starts looking patchy or dull the finish has already gone. Use a barely damp cloth and dry immediately, or a cleaner made for leather.

#### How do you clean a leather sofa at home?

Dust it weekly with a dry microfibre cloth, vacuum the crevices monthly with a soft brush attachment rather than a hard nozzle, and wipe over occasionally with a cloth wrung out in clean water so it is barely damp, drying it straight away with a second cloth. Blot spills rather than rubbing. Avoid household sprays, solvents, silicone polish and kitchen remedies entirely.

#### Can scratches be removed from leather?

On aniline and semi-aniline leather, light scratches often fade if you warm them with a fingertip and buff gently with a soft cloth, because the hide is dyed all the way through. On pigmented leather a scratch that has broken the surface finish reveals a different colour beneath and will not buff out — that needs a leather refinisher to fill and recolour, which is a routine job for them.

## I don't want this job — how do I say no? — https://www.learntoupholster.com/business/saying-no-to-a-job

### How do I turn down work without damaging my reputation?

Decline quickly, politely, and without a detailed justification. "I'm afraid it's not something I can take on" is a complete sentence and needs no defence. Do not price yourself out instead of refusing, because sometimes people say yes. Do not go quiet and hope they lose interest, because that is what makes people leave reviews. If you can name someone better suited, do — a good referral turns a refusal into a favour.

### Why this is hard

Turning work away feels wrong, especially early on. There is always the thought that the diary might be empty in three months and you will regret it.

But the jobs you do not want are rarely just unappealing. They are usually unprofitable, awkward, or attached to somebody who is going to be difficult, and those three tend to travel together. Taking them costs you the capacity to do work you actually want.

### The mistake almost everyone makes first

Quoting a silly number to make them go away.

It fails in both directions. Sometimes they say yes, and now you are committed to the job you did not want, at a price that has made the customer's expectations enormous. And sometimes they tell people you quoted an outrageous figure, which is a worse outcome than simply having said no.

If you do not want the work, refuse it. Do not price it.

### How to actually say it

Short, warm, prompt, no reasons.

> "Thanks for thinking of me. I'm afraid it's not something I can take on at the moment — I hope you find someone who can help."

That is enough. The urge to explain is strong and should be resisted, because every reason you give is something the customer can argue with. "I'm too busy" invites *when are you free?* "It's not really my sort of work" invites *but could you have a look anyway?*

No reason, no argument.

### Refer if you can

The single best thing you can do is point them somewhere useful.

> "It's not something I take on, but [name] does a lot of that sort of work and is worth a call."

You have now solved their problem without doing the job. People remember that, and it is how referrals come back to you later. If you cannot think of anyone, the [find an upholsterer](https://www.learntoupholster.com/find-an-upholsterer) page is a reasonable thing to point at.

### The ones worth declining

Patterns that come up repeatedly:

- Furniture with no structural future — chipboard frames, stapled softwood, anything not worth the labour

- A customer who has already fallen out with another upholsterer

- Fabric you have advised against and they insist on anyway

- Work you have not done before, at a price that leaves no room to learn on it

- Anything where the person is haggling before you have even quoted



That last one is the clearest signal in the trade. Someone negotiating before they know the price is telling you what the whole job will be like.

### Say it early

The cost of declining rises every day you leave it. A refusal on the first phone call is a minor disappointment. A refusal after two weeks of silence, three chasing emails and a site visit is a grievance.

### Also worth reading

- [Pricing and quoting](https://www.learntoupholster.com/pricing-and-quoting)

Anonymous, about three minutes. [Add your workshop](https://www.learntoupholster.com/state-of-the-trade/take-part).

## I'm busy but I'm not making money — https://www.learntoupholster.com/business/busy-but-not-making-money

### Why am I fully booked and still broke?

Almost always because your hourly rate is set from what you hope customers will pay rather than what the workshop costs to run. Work out your true cost per bench hour first: overheads plus the wage you need, divided by the hours you can actually charge for. Most upholsterers can only bill 55 to 65 per cent of the hours they work, because stripping, collecting, quoting and buying materials are not billable. Being fully booked at a rate below that number just means losing money faster.

### The arithmetic nobody does

A full order book feels like success. It is the most common way a workshop goes under.

The trap is that being busy hides the problem. Money keeps arriving, so the bank balance never collapses dramatically enough to force a reckoning. It just never grows, and you work harder each year to stand still.

Here is the calculation almost nobody does before setting a rate.

Add up what the workshop costs you in a year whether or not you do any work: rent, rates, insurance, power, phone, van, accountant, subscriptions, tools and replacement of them. Then add the wage you actually need to live on. That total is what the business must generate before it has made a penny.

Now the part that catches people. Divide that by your *billable* hours, not your working hours.

### Billable hours are not working hours

You cannot charge for all the time you spend. Stripping a chair is billable. Driving to collect it usually is not. Quoting is not. Ordering fabric is not. Chasing a supplier who sent the wrong batch is definitely not. Nor is the hour spent photographing finished work, or doing the books, or standing in the workshop deciding what to do first.

> In a one-person workshop, expect to bill 55 to 65 per cent of the hours you work. If you are also doing your own marketing and admin, it will be nearer the bottom of that range.

So a forty-hour week is realistically twenty-two to twenty-six chargeable hours. If you set your rate by dividing your costs across forty, you have under-priced everything by roughly forty per cent, and no amount of extra work will fix it. It makes it worse.

### The symptoms

You can usually spot this before the accounts confirm it.

- You are booked months ahead but dread looking at the bank

- You cannot take a week off without it hurting

- You quote a job, win it immediately, and feel uneasy about how quickly they agreed

- Jobs routinely take half as long again as you estimated

- You are buying materials out of the next customer's deposit



That last one is the serious signal. Once deposits are funding the previous job's materials, the workshop is running on borrowed time and one cancellation can bring it down.

### Fixing it without losing every customer

Raise the rate. That is the fix. The question is only how.

1. Work out the real number first, using the calculation above. Do not guess at it.

2. Apply the new rate to every quote from a fixed date. Do not renegotiate work already agreed.

3. Do not announce it. Nobody sends a letter about their prices going up; you just quote the new figure.

4. Expect to lose some enquiries. That is the mechanism working, not a sign it has failed.



The customers you lose at a higher rate are, almost without exception, the ones who were costing you money. The ones who stay are the ones who wanted the work done properly.

> Underquoting is the apprentice's mistake. Doing it for twenty years is a business model, and a bad one.

### The one that is harder to hear

If the real number comes out well above what your local market will pay, the answer is not to work for less. It is that you are selling the wrong thing to the wrong people.

That usually means moving up: better pieces, traditional work, trade and contract clients, designers, or teaching. All of those pay properly for skill. Competing on price against a workshop that staples foam over the old cover is a race you cannot win and should not enter.

Anonymous, about three minutes. [Add your workshop](https://www.learntoupholster.com/state-of-the-trade/take-part).

## Industrial sewing for upholsterers — https://www.learntoupholster.com/sewing

Industrial sewing explained for upholsterers. Most of what is written about these machines is aimed at sailmakers, leatherworkers or garment factories — this is the same ground from an upholstery bench.

### Thread

Bonded nylon or polyester, Tex sizes and the three numbering systems, which thread for which job, and the twist question.

### Needles

Needle size by thread size, needle systems, round and leather points, and why a blunt needle causes skipped stitches.

### Thread & needle selector

Answer three questions and get the thread, size, needle and stitch length for the job.

### Machines

Walking foot, compound and needle feed, cylinder arm, flat bed — explained for upholsterers rather than sailmakers.

### Troubleshooting

Fraying, skipped stitches, uneven tension, puckering, thread breaks.

### Setup & parts

Presser feet, servo against clutch motors, speed reducers, tension and timing.

**Where to start.** If something is going wrong at the machine, it is thread or needle far more often than tension. The two guides above answer most of it, and the pairing between them answers most of the rest.

This section is being built out. Thread and needles are done; the selector, machines, troubleshooting and setup follow.

## Industrial sewing machines for upholstery — https://www.learntoupholster.com/sewing-machines

Two things describe a machine: how it moves the material, and what shape the bed is. The first matters far more than the second, and it is the one most buying guides skate over.

**The short version.** For upholstery you want a **compound feed** machine on a **flat bed**. Everything else on this page is either a step down from that or a specialist you will use a handful of times a year.

### Feed — how the material is moved

A machine has to move two surfaces of the material at the same rate. If it only drives the underside, the top creeps, and on a long seam you finish with the two pieces out of register. That is the single most common reason upholstery sewn on the wrong machine looks wrong.

#### Drop feed Regular feed

not upholstery

How it works

Feed dogs under the material do all the work, moving it while the needle is out of the fabric. The presser foot only holds down.

Good for

Single layers of cloth. Every domestic machine and the lighter industrials.

Where it falls down

Anything thick, layered, or slippery. The top layer creeps and you finish a long seam with the two pieces out of register — the classic result of sewing upholstery on the wrong machine.

#### Needle feed

better

How it works

The needle moves with the feed dogs rather than straight up and down, so it carries the material forward while it is still through it.

Good for

Thicker seams than drop feed will manage. Keeps layers in register better.

Where it falls down

Still nothing gripping the top surface, so slippery materials can drift.

#### Walking foot Top feed

good

How it works

An alternating pair of feet. The outer foot holds while the inner foot lifts, moves forward, drops and grips — so the top of the material is driven as well as the bottom.

Good for

Vinyl, coated cloth, single-layer leather, most upholstery panels. Stops the top layer drifting.

Where it falls down

The needle still does not move with the material, so heavy multi-layer assemblies can shift at the point where you turn a corner.

#### Compound feed Unison feed · triple feed · compound walking foot

what you want

How it works

Feed dogs, inner foot and **needle** all move together while the outer foot holds. Three things driving the material in step instead of one.

Good for

This is the upholstery machine. Thick multi-layer work, leather, heavy weaves, anything where the layers must stay in register through a curve.

Where it falls down

Poor on very light cloth — the feed can mark delicate material. Less forgiving to set up than a drop feed, and it takes practice to get the settings right for a new material.

**The names are used inconsistently, so here is a test that settles it.** One supplier calls unison feed “also known as walking foot feed”. Another says needle feed “is more appropriately termed compound”. A third lists compound, needle and triple feed as three names for one thing. They are not the same thing.

Watch the needle as the machine sews. **If the needle moves forward with the material, it is compound feed.** If the needle only goes up and down while the top foot walks, it is a walking foot machine and nothing more. That is checkable in ten seconds and it beats arguing about the label on the box.

### Bed — what shape the machine is

The bed decides what you can physically get under the needle. It has nothing to do with how well the machine sews.

#### Flat bed

The familiar shape: a flat table with the needle in the middle.

Good for

Long straight seams over big panels. Everything flat, which in upholstery is most things. The workhorse, and the machine to buy first.

Where it falls down

Useless on anything tubular or three-dimensional. You cannot get inside a finished cushion cover or round a headrest.

#### Cylinder arm

The bed is a narrow horizontal cylinder rather than a table, so work can be fed round it.

Good for

Tubular and three-dimensional work — headrests, bolsters, finished covers, awkward corners a flat bed cannot reach.

Where it falls down

Long flat seams are harder to keep straight with no table to rest on. Flat-bed attachments exist to convert one, which is worth knowing before you buy two machines.

#### Post bed

The needle sits on top of a raised vertical post.

Good for

Visibility and control on small, detailed, three-dimensional pieces. Precision top stitching where you need to see exactly where the needle lands.

Where it falls down

A specialist. Very few upholstery jobs actually need one.

#### Long arm

A flat bed stretched — more room to the right of the needle.

Good for

Large panels, awnings, tarpaulins, marine covers. Anything where the bulk of the work has to pass through the throat.

Where it falls down

Takes up a great deal of bench. Only worth it if you regularly handle pieces big enough to fight a standard machine.

### The overlocker

Worth its own mention because it does a job the walking foot machine cannot, and because a lot of upholsterers do not realise how much use it gets.

An overlocker sews, trims and wraps the raw edge in one pass, using loopers instead of a bobbin. In upholstery it is edge protection: it stops a cut edge unravelling before you have got the piece together.

**Only on cloth that actually frays.** Plenty of upholstery weaves are stable enough at the cut edge that overlocking them is time spent for nothing. It earns its keep on loose weaves, nubby textures, linens and anything destined for a loose cover that will be taken off and washed.

**The order that works.** Overlock the cut pieces first, then straight stitch them together on the walking foot machine.

Doing it that way you are running flat single layers through the overlocker, which is quick and accurate. Leave it until after the seam is sewn and you are feeding a bulky folded allowance through instead, on a curve, with the piece already assembled. Both methods are used, but the first is easier on every count.

**The overlock is not the seam.** On woven cloth, an overlocked join on its own can fray along with the edge or sit oddly on the face side. The straight stitch is what holds the piece together; the overlock only protects the raw edge. A five-thread overlocker does both in one pass — a four-thread does not.

### What to actually buy

**One compound feed flat bed machine will do almost everything.** Long seams, panels, cushions, covers, leather, vinyl, heavy weaves. If you buy one machine, buy that.

**What is actually in my workshop, after thirty-four years.** Two walking foot machines — a Jack kept for the thick work and a Juki for everything else — plus an overlocker, and a second Jack that lives in the van for on-site repairs. No cylinder arm. No post bed.

That is worth saying plainly because every buying guide points you at a specialist bed as the second machine. In practice the second machine that earns its keep is *another flat bed*, because what you are really buying is a second setup: one threaded heavy with a big needle, one ready for ordinary work, and no stopping to change over.

The forums say the same thing from the other direction. Upholsterers who do own cylinder and post bed machines report they make small curved work easier but only on a few seams, and not often — one trimmer noting it is less trouble to top stitch on the flat bed already threaded than to swap thread over to the cylinder for two runs. Flat-bed attachments exist for cylinder machines, so if the awkward work is occasional there is a cheaper way round it than a second head.

The exception is genuinely three-dimensional work most days — a lot of headrests, bolsters or finished covers going round the arm. Then a cylinder arm stops being a luxury. For most furniture upholstery it never quite gets there.

Thread and needles for whatever you end up with: [the selector](https://www.learntoupholster.com/sewing-selector), [thread guide](https://www.learntoupholster.com/sewing-thread) and [needle guide](https://www.learntoupholster.com/sewing-needles).

Sizing is standardised, so these numbers hold wherever you work. Manufacturers do vary slightly at the margins, though — if your thread supplier publishes a chart for their own product, it beats any general table including this one.

## Insurance for an upholstery workshop — https://www.learntoupholster.com/business/insurance-for-an-upholstery-workshop

### What insurance does an upholsterer actually need?

More than most workshops carry, and in a different shape than they expect. Public liability is the one everybody buys — but it usually excludes damage to property in your care, custody and control, which is exactly what a workshop full of customers' furniture is. That gap is the one most upholsterers do not know they have. We started on £1m public liability, went to £5m when a holiday park contract required it, and added more again for teaching. Tools are covered both in the workshop and on site.

### What we carry, and how it grew

Worth setting out plainly, because the shape of it changed as the business did.

**We started with £1 million public liability.** That is the standard starting point and it was fine for domestic work out of a workshop.

**Then a holiday park contract required £5 million.** Large operators run approved contractor lists and set their own minimum, and £1m or £2m will not get you on one. That was not a choice — it was the price of the work.

**Teaching meant adding more again.** Students on the premises, using machines and sharp tools, is a different risk from me working alone, and the policy had to reflect it.

**Tools are insured in the workshop and on site**, everything from sewing machines to staple guns. On-site cover matters as soon as any of your work happens away from the bench.

Three upgrades in the life of one business. Which is really the point of this article: the cover you bought when you started stops matching the business you have.

> None of this is insurance advice — I am an upholsterer, not a broker, and the rules and names differ from country to country. Treat it as a list of things to ask about.

### Public liability, and what it does not cover

Public liability covers injury to other people, and damage to other people's property, arising out of your business. A customer trips over a trailing lead in your workshop. You drop a sofa through their bay window on the way in.

Here is the part that catches people.

**Most public liability policies exclude property in your care, custody and control.**

Read that against what an upholstery workshop actually is: a building containing several thousand pounds' worth of other people's furniture, all of it in your care, custody and control, most of it irreplaceable.

If your workshop floods, or burns, or is broken into, public liability will not pay for your customers' sofas. That is not the policy failing. It is the policy working exactly as written, and it is the single biggest gap in this trade.

### The cover nobody asks for by name

What you need for that is a separate thing, usually sold as **goods in trust**, **customers' goods**, or **bailee cover**. Different insurers call it different things, which is part of why people miss it.

Ask three questions about it:

1. **What is the limit?** Add up what is genuinely in your workshop on a busy week, including anything waiting to be collected. Most people underestimate this badly. Three sofas and a suite is a serious number.

2. **Does it cover goods in transit?** You collect and deliver. Furniture on the back of the van is still your responsibility and is not always included.

3. **Does it cover goods at the customer's premises?** If you work on site — holiday parks, venues, heritage properties — the piece never enters your workshop but is still in your hands.



This is also where a written condition report earns its keep. If there is ever an argument about whether damage was already there, a signed record made before work started is the difference between a conversation and a claim. There is a printable one in the [workshop forms](https://www.learntoupholster.com/workshop-forms).

### Product liability

Usually bundled with public liability, and worth understanding separately for this trade.

Product liability covers harm caused by what you have supplied. For an upholsterer that mostly means one thing: **fire**. If a piece you recovered is implicated in a fire, the question of what you fitted and whether it complied will be asked, and it will be asked of you.

Two things follow.

Keep the certificates. Every foam, every cloth, every wadding, filed against the job. A policy will not help you evidence compliance — only your records will.

And a policy is unlikely to help at all if you knowingly worked outside the specification. That is one of the reasons I turned down [the 76-chair contract](https://www.learntoupholster.com/business/the-contract-i-turned-down): being told to do it that way is not a defence, and I would not want to test whether my insurer agreed.

### Employers' liability

In the UK this is a legal requirement the moment you employ anyone, with a statutory minimum of £5 million. Most policies are written at £10m.

The trap is who counts as employed. Casual help, a friend who comes in on Saturdays, someone on a trial, and in some circumstances family members can all bring the obligation into play. It is not only about people on a formal contract.

If you take on an apprentice, a student on placement, or anyone at all who works under your direction, ask the question before they start rather than after.

Employment rules vary enormously by country. This is one to check locally rather than assume.

### Tools, equipment and the van

Straightforward in principle and full of exclusions in practice.

Insure the tools for what it would cost to replace them, and be honest about the total — machines, compressor, hand tools, the lot. It adds up faster than most people think.

Then ask about **on-site and in-transit cover**, which is separate from workshop cover on many policies. If you work at holiday parks or customers' premises, or keep a machine in the van as I do, this is not optional.

And ask specifically about **tools left in a vehicle overnight**. A great many policies exclude this outright, or require the van to be in a locked garage, or cap it at a low figure. Trades discover this after a break-in rather than before. If your van is parked on the road with a machine in it, find out tonight what your policy actually says.

### Two that get overlooked

**Business interruption.** If a fire or flood stops you working for three months, your income stops with it while the overheads carry on. Cover for lost earnings is the difference between a bad year and the end of the business. Ask what it would actually pay and for how long.

**Vehicle work.** If you do campervan or vehicle trimming and customers' vehicles come to you — or you drive them at all, even a few yards to reposition them — check whether that is covered. Working on somebody's vehicle and being responsible for somebody's vehicle are different things to an insurer, and standard workshop cover may not extend to it.

### Tell them everything

The most important habit is disclosure, because non-disclosure is how policies fail at exactly the moment you need them.

Tell your insurer, in writing:

- What proportion of your work is contract or commercial rather than domestic

- That you work at customers' premises, if you do

- That you teach or take students, if you do

- That you handle vehicles, if you do

- That you store customers' goods, and roughly how much

- What machinery is on the premises

- Anything at all that has changed since the policy was written



An insurer who knows all of that and prices for it will pay. An insurer who finds out at claim stage may not.

### Review it every year

The £1m to £5m story is the whole argument for this.

Nothing about our insurance was wrong when we bought it. It simply stopped describing the business, because the business changed — contract work arrived, then teaching, then on-site work and vehicles.

Put a reminder in the diary for the same week every year and read the schedule properly rather than renewing on autopilot. Ten minutes, once a year, on the document that decides whether one bad day ends the business.

### The short version

If you take only two things from this:

**Public liability probably does not cover your customers' furniture.** Find out today whether you have goods in trust cover and what the limit is.

**Tell your insurer everything you do.** Every article in this Business Hub about growing into new work — [holiday parks](https://www.learntoupholster.com/business/caravan-and-holiday-park-work), teaching, [commercial clients](https://www.learntoupholster.com/business/winning-contract-clients) — is also a reason to ring your broker before you start.

### Tools for this

- [Workshop forms](https://www.learntoupholster.com/workshop-forms)

- [Winning contract clients](https://www.learntoupholster.com/business/winning-contract-clients)

- [The contract i turned down](https://www.learntoupholster.com/business/the-contract-i-turned-down)

Anonymous, about three minutes. [Add your workshop](https://www.learntoupholster.com/state-of-the-trade/take-part).

## Ireland upholstery fire regulations — https://www.learntoupholster.com/fire-regulations-ireland

Its own 1995 Order and Irish Standard, close to the British regime but a separate legal instrument.

**Written by a British upholsterer.** This is informational guidance rather than legal advice, and I work in England. Every statement is sourced and the sources are listed at the foot of the page — check them, and where a job carries real risk get the requirement confirmed in writing by whoever is responsible for the premises.

### Domestic work

Required by law

**S.I. No. 316/1995 and Irish Standard IS 419**

#### A separate Irish instrument

The Industrial Research and Standards (Fire Safety) (Domestic Furniture) Order 1995 (S.I. No. 316/1995), with Irish Standard **IS 419**, sets fire resistance levels for domestic upholstered furniture. It is not the British regulations, and a piece compliant in Britain is not automatically compliant here.

#### European test methods

The tests are the EN series familiar across Europe: **EN 1021-1** for a smouldering cigarette and **EN 1021-2** for match flame equivalent. These are the same tests British upholsterers know as BS EN 1021.

#### Northern Ireland is different again

Northern Ireland follows the UK Furniture and Furnishings (Fire) (Safety) Regulations, not the Irish Order, alongside EU General Product Safety requirements. If you work across the border, they are two regimes.

#### Check the current position before you rely on it

The Irish regulations have been under review, and the Department of Enterprise has consulted on amending them. Verify the current requirement rather than relying on this page alone.

### Commercial and contract work

Depends on the building

**EN 1021 as the baseline, with the building setting the rest**

#### Public premises are specified more strictly

Contract and public seating requirements come from the building’s fire safety obligations rather than from the domestic furniture Order.

#### BS 7176 is widely used

Much contract fabric supplied into Ireland is tested and certificated to the British contract standard, so BS 7176 hazard categories and crib 5 appear routinely in Irish specifications.

#### Ask the responsible person

As everywhere: get the required category in writing before you cut anything.

**Sources.**

- [S.I. No. 316/1995 — Irish Statute Book](https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/1995/si/316/)

- [Furniture fire regulations consultation — Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment](https://enterprise.gov.ie/en/consultations/furniture-fire-regulations-consultation.html)



Last checked 2026-08-02. Fire rules change — verify before you rely on this.

[All countries](https://www.learntoupholster.com/fire-regulations) · [United Kingdom checker](https://www.learntoupholster.com/fire-safety-checker)

## Is it cheaper to reupholster or buy new? — https://www.learntoupholster.com/blog/is-it-cheaper-to-reupholster-or-buy-new

### Is reupholstering cheaper than buying a new sofa?

Compared with the cheapest new sofa in a sale, usually not. Compared with a new sofa of the same quality as the one you already own, very often yes — and that is the comparison that matters. A budget sofa is a stapled softwood frame with a life measured in single-figure years; a well-made frame is hardwood, jointed, and can be recovered several times over a lifetime. So the question is never really about price. It is about what your frame is made of, and you can settle that by turning the sofa over and looking underneath.

This is the most common question in the trade and the one most often answered badly, usually by somebody with an interest in the answer. So here is how I would work it out if it were my sofa.

### The comparison almost everybody makes is the wrong one

It goes like this. A quote comes back at some number. The person then finds a new sofa in a sale for less than that number, and the maths looks like it has answered itself.

But those two things are not comparable. What you are really being offered is a choice between repairing something you already own and buying something different — and the something different is, almost always, a considerably lesser object.

A budget new sofa is built to a price that has to cover timber, foam, fabric, assembly, a shipping container from the Far East, a warehouse, a showroom, a salesperson, a delivery van and a profit margin. Something has to give, and what gives is the frame: softwood, stapled, often with no centre support across a long seat. It is designed to look right in a showroom and to last a certain number of years, and it usually does exactly that.

The sofa you already own may be built the same way — in which case, fine, the sums are what they are. Or it may be hardwood, jointed, forty years old and structurally good for another forty. Recovering that is not the same transaction at all.

### Check the frame. It decides everything.

Two minutes, and you do not need any tools.

- Turn it over, or tip it up. Look at the timber in the frame where you can see it, and at the dust cover fixings.

- Look at the joints. Corner blocks, dowels, screws or proper mortise-and-tenon joints mean a frame built to last. Butt joints held with staples and a squirt of glue mean it was not.

- Look at the timber. Hardwood is dense, close-grained and heavy. Softwood is pale, open-grained, and often visibly a construction-grade batten.

- Lift one end. Crude, but weight is a decent proxy. Good frames are heavy. If one person can lift a three-seater easily, that tells you something.

- Sight along the front edge. If it dips in the middle, the frame is already flexing under load.

A hardwood, jointed, sound frame is worth recovering nearly every time. A stapled softwood frame that is already bowing is telling you to let it go.

### When reupholstery clearly wins

- The frame is good. As above. This is the whole argument in one line.

- You cannot buy the shape any more. Period pieces, show-wood chairs, anything with a proper sprung seat. Nothing currently in a showroom is a replacement for a Howard-style armchair or a Victorian nursing chair — you can only buy a modern approximation, usually at a price that makes recovering look sensible.

- It fits. If a piece was made for the alcove it sits in, or is the only thing that gets round your staircase, that is worth real money.

- You want a particular fabric. A new sofa comes with a menu of perhaps eight options. Recovering opens the entire fabric trade to you — thousands of cloths, any weight, any colour, at whatever price you choose to spend.

- It matters to you. The chair somebody sat in. There is no arithmetic for that and it is a perfectly good reason on its own.

- You want it to be right underneath. Recovering is the moment the foam gets specified properly, the webbing gets renewed and the frame gets repaired. You are not just changing the cover.

### When buying new is the better call

I turn work away on all of these, and I would rather say so here than in a workshop with somebody's sofa already stripped.

- Cheap stapled frame, already failing. Repairing it costs more than it is worth and will not hold.

- Reclining and electric mechanisms. On a recliner the mechanism is the value. If that is what has failed, recovering the outside does not help you, and parts for older models are frequently unobtainable.

- Very large corner units. Fabric quantity and labour both scale badly. A corner sofa takes around 22 metres of cloth against 16 for a three-seater, before anyone has been paid to fit it.

- You do not actually like the shape. This sounds obvious and it catches people constantly. Recovering gives you the same sofa in a different colour. If the shape has always been slightly wrong, it will still be slightly wrong, and you will have paid to keep it.

### What actually drives the price

It helps to know where the money goes, because it explains why two quotes can differ so widely.

Fabric quantity times fabric price. This is the single biggest variable and it is entirely in your hands. A three-seat sofa takes roughly 16 metres of 137cm cloth; a two-seater around 13; a club armchair about 6. Multiply that by the difference between a modest cloth and a designer one and you have a swing of many hundreds of pounds on the same job. Our yardage calculator will give you a figure for your piece before you go anywhere near a fabric shop.

What is underneath. New foam, new webbing, spring repairs, frame work. Necessary, and it is the part that determines whether the finished piece is actually any good.

Complexity. Deep buttoning, piping, pattern matching, show wood to be stripped and polished, loose covers rather than fixed. Each adds hours.

Labour. Stripping alone on an old piece can take the best part of a day, and it is done before anything visible has happened.

The cost estimator will put a range around your piece. Treat it as a way of knowing whether a quote is sane, not as a quote.

### The pattern-repeat trap

One thing worth knowing before you fall in love with a fabric. Anything with a pattern repeat, and any one-way cloth such as velvet, needs more metreage than a plain — sometimes considerably more, because panels cannot be turned or nested efficiently in the cutting plan.

People choose a cloth on price per metre, then discover the job needs several extra metres of it. Ask for the quantity for that specific fabric before committing.

### The bit that does not appear in the sums

Something in the order of 22 million pieces of furniture are discarded in the UK every year — a figure that traces back to a North London Waste Authority report, alongside WRAP's estimate of roughly 670,000 tonnes annually. More than half of it is reckoned to be still usable or easily repairable when it is thrown out. A frame that gets recovered twice has done the work of three sofas.

I mention it last rather than first because I do not think it should be the deciding argument — but if the numbers land close together, it is a reasonable thumb on the scale.

### The short version

Turn the sofa over. If the frame is hardwood and properly jointed, recovering it will almost certainly give you a better piece of furniture than anything you could buy for the same money, and you get to choose the cloth. If it is stapled softwood and already sagging, thank it for its service.

Everything else — fabric, foam, complexity — is detail you can adjust. The frame is the thing you cannot change.

### Common questions

#### Is it cheaper to reupholster a sofa than buy a new one?

Compared with a budget new sofa, generally no. Compared with a new sofa of equivalent build quality, generally yes. The comparison only makes sense if both sides are the same standard of furniture: a stapled softwood frame has a life measured in single-figure years, while a hardwood jointed frame can be recovered several times over decades. The frame you already own decides which comparison applies.

#### How do I know if my sofa is worth reupholstering?

Look at the frame. Turn the piece over and check whether the joints are dowelled, screwed, blocked or properly jointed rather than butted and stapled, whether the timber is dense hardwood rather than pale softwood, and whether the front edge dips in the middle when you sight along it. A sound hardwood frame is worth recovering; a stapled softwood frame that is already flexing is not.

#### How much fabric does a sofa need to be reupholstered?

As a starting figure, roughly 16 metres of 137cm cloth for a three-seat sofa, 13 for a two-seater, around 6 for a club armchair and about 22 for a corner unit. Patterned fabrics and one-way cloths such as velvet need more, because the panels cannot be turned or nested efficiently when cutting. Always measure the actual piece before buying expensive cloth.

#### Is it worth reupholstering a recliner?

Usually not, if the problem is the mechanism, because on a recliner the mechanism is where the value sits and replacement parts for older models are often unobtainable. If the mechanism works perfectly and only the covering has worn, recovering can make sense — but expect it to cost more than a fixed chair of the same size, because the moving parts complicate every stage.

## Jensen S-V8 — Fitting a New Car Carpet Set in Navy — Upholstery Project — https://www.learntoupholster.com/projects/jensen-s-v8-carpet-set

### Stripped out — down to the bare floor

The cabin opened up: seats and trims away, the last of the old red carpet still on the tunnel, bare floor underneath.
This is where a carpet job actually starts, and it is more dismantling than upholstery. Seats out, seat belts unbolted, sills and kick panels off, centre console away, gear lever gaiter and handbrake boot released. Every fixing you take out is one you have to find again on the way back, and every trim that laps over a carpet edge is telling you the order things have to go in. Strip it in sequence and photograph as you go, because nobody remembers which of four similar screws came out of which hole three days later.

### The old red carpet — the only pattern that exists

This is the whole job in one photograph. That worn red panel is not rubbish, it is the pattern, and it is the only one that will ever exist for this car. Look at what it already carries: the finished bound edge along the top, the round aperture cut for the gear lever, the stepped notch where it clears the bulkhead, and the scalloped bottom edge shaped to sit under the sill trim. Every one of those was worked out at the factory in 2002 and none of it has to be worked out again — it just has to be copied accurately. So it comes out as intact as it can be persuaded to come, gets brushed off, and goes on the bench face up. Before anything else it is marked: which panel, which way up, which way the pile runs, and where the centreline falls. Then it is laid on the flat navy carpet and cut round with a working allowance on the edges that will finish under a trim. The dirt and wear you can see along the bottom of this piece is exactly why it was being replaced — and exactly why it needed photographing before it went in the bin.

### Back together in the workshop

The cabin rebuilt on 23 July, new navy carpet down and the interior refitted over it.
With the patterns laid on flat automotive carpet and cut round with a working allowance, the new panels went in. The transmission tunnel is where these jobs are won or lost — it is a compound curve, falling away in two directions at once, and flat carpet will not sit on it without the relief cuts the old panel shows you. Everything was dry-fitted first: laid in, pressed into the tunnel, checked against the console mountings and the gear lever aperture, and only then glued. High-temperature contact adhesive gives you one attempt, so the dry fit is the job rather than a formality.

### On the field, nine days later

The car at a show on 1 August, roof down and the whole cabin open to view.
Nine days after the workshop photograph the car was on a show field with the roof folded — which is the real test of a carpet job, because a convertible has nowhere to hide. Every trimmed edge and every shade difference in the pile is out in daylight for anybody who cares to lean over the door, and at a show plenty of people do exactly that.

### Navy against black leather and alloy

The driver's footwell and tunnel, navy running up to the console and switch panel.
Colour choice matters as much as workmanship. The original red had gone flat and pink with age and fought with the lilac-blue paintwork; navy sits under the black leather and the brushed alloy switch panel without arguing with either, and it answers the exterior colour instead of clashing with it. It is a quiet decision that makes a cabin look deliberate, and it costs nothing extra at the point of ordering.

### One continuous run

Both footwells, the tunnel and the console surround — one continuous run of navy.
This is the view that shows whether the patterning was honest. The carpet runs from footwell to tunnel to console without a break in tone or a rippled edge, the console and gear gaiter sit down on it properly, and the seat rails clear it as they were always meant to. Nothing here is a new shape: it is what the factory cut, copied off the originals and made again in a better colour. It also answers the question about pile direction — every panel was laid on the roll the same way up before cutting, because carpet cut with the nap running two ways reads as two different shades of navy the moment sunlight gets into the car.

### The seat, the belt anchor and the carpet edge

The seat refitted, belt anchored, and the carpet running cleanly under the runners and up to the sill.
Refitting is not simply the reverse of stripping. Seat belt anchor bolts are a safety-critical fixing and go back to the manufacturer's torque, with the carpet trimmed clear of the mounting face rather than trapped under it — carpet caught under a load-bearing washer compresses over time and lets the fixing slacken. The seat runners bolt to their original captive points, the carpet is relieved around them, and the sill trim goes back last to cover the cut edge.

### The methods behind this job

Every technique used here is set out in full in the book:

- [Stripping the Old Work](https://www.learntoupholster.com/stripping-the-old-work)

- [Materials — A Field Guide](https://www.learntoupholster.com/materials-a-field-guide)

- [Trimming & Finishing](https://www.learntoupholster.com/trimming-and-finishing)

- [Work out the material for your own job](https://www.learntoupholster.com/fabric-yardage)



### Questions about this job

#### How do you pattern a car carpet set if you cannot buy a moulded one?

You use the old carpet. Strip the interior right back, lift the original out in as few pieces as possible, and it becomes your pattern set — it already carries every relief cut, every seat-rail aperture and every trimmed edge the factory worked out. Before anything moves, mark each piece: which panel it is, which way up, which way the pile runs, and where the centreline falls. Then lay each old panel on the new carpet and cut round it with a working allowance at the edges that will be hidden by trim. On rare or low-volume cars this is the only method available, because nobody makes a moulded set for a car built in tens rather than tens of thousands.

#### What glue should you use to stick carpet into a car?

High-temperature contact adhesive, the vehicle-grade sort rated to around 120°C. A car standing in summer sun reaches temperatures that soften ordinary contact adhesive, and once it softens the carpet creeps, lifts at the edges and bubbles across the tunnel. Coat both faces, let them flash off until touch-dry, then bond — it grabs on contact, so position everything with a dry fit first. Where a trim, sill or kick panel laps over a carpet edge, let it do its share of the holding rather than asking the adhesive to carry a raw edge on its own.

#### Does the pile direction of car carpet matter?

Yes, and it is the mistake that shows up in daylight rather than in the workshop. Automotive carpet has a nap, so light reflects differently depending on which way the pile lies. Two panels cut from the same roll but laid opposite ways will read as two different shades of navy, black or grey once the sun gets into the cabin, and no amount of good fitting will disguise it. Mark the pile direction on every pattern piece as it comes out, and lay every new piece on the roll the same way up before cutting.

#### Do the seats have to come out to fit a new car carpet?

For a proper job, yes — along with the seat belts, sills, kick panels, centre console and any trim that laps a carpet edge. Carpet cut around fixed seats has to be slit to get it in, and those slits are visible for the rest of the car's life. Taking the interior out also lets you see and clean the floor, which is where the useful discoveries are made: damp underfelt, surface rust, a blocked drain channel. Refitting is where the care is needed rather than the speed — seat belt anchors and seat runners are safety-critical fixings and go back to the correct torque, with the carpet trimmed clear of the mounting faces rather than trapped underneath them.

#### How long does it take to fit a new car carpet set?

This one was ten hours from start to finish — stripping the interior, lifting and marking the old carpet, cutting the new panels, gluing them in and refitting everything over the top. That is a fair figure for a small two-seater with a simple floor. Expect more on a four-seat car, on anything with a complicated console or rear seat arrangement, and on any car where the old carpet has to be recovered in pieces rather than lifted out whole. The fitting itself is the quick part; the stripping and the patterning are where the hours go, and rushing either is what produces the jobs you can spot from the doorway.

#### What is a Jensen S-V8?

A two-seat British roadster, the last production car to carry the Jensen name. It was launched at the 1998 motor show and eventually built at Speke on Merseyside from August 2001, using a 4.6-litre Ford V8 in a steel monocoque under pressed aluminium panels. Only about twenty cars left the factory before Jensen went into administration in July 2002; the part-built cars were sold on and finished afterwards, giving a total of fewer than fifty. That rarity is exactly why the original carpet had to come out in one piece — there is no catalogue to order a replacement set from.

### Have a piece like this?

Find a professional upholsterer near you — UK, US and worldwide — to bring your own chair, sofa or piece back to life.

## Kawasaki Motorbike Seat in Diamond-Stitch Vinyl — Upholstery Project — https://www.learntoupholster.com/projects/kawasaki-motorbike-seat

### The seat as it came in

The seat as it came in — the original ribbed vinyl cover, tired and splitting at the nose.
The seat arrived straight off the bike: the original pleated vinyl cover, decades old, hard and splitting where it wraps the nose. The cover itself was past saving, but that is not why it came in — the owner wanted rid of the stepped factory shape altogether. When the shape is changing, the old cover is only useful for one thing: telling you how the factory got their cover on and off the pan, which tells you how yours will go on too.

### Stripped and reshaped flat

Stripped back and rebuilt with new foam, cut to the flat profile the customer asked for.
Old cover off, and the foam cut back and rebuilt to the new shape. Because the customer wanted the seat flat, the new foam goes on as a level top rather than following the old stepped profile — new sheet foam bonded down and trimmed square along the sides, with a firmer section at the tail where a passenger sits. The original metal pan underneath is sound, so it stays: all the fixings and mounting points are untouched and the seat will bolt straight back onto the bike.

### Patterning with shrink wrap

The reshaped seat wrapped tight in shrink wrap, with the seam lines and balance marks drawn on.
With a brand-new shape, there is no old cover to copy — so the pattern comes off the seat itself. The whole seat gets wrapped tight in layers of shrink wrap until it forms a firm skin, then the seam lines go on in marker: where the top panel meets the sides, where the piping will run, plus balance marks across the seams so every panel goes back together in exactly the right place at the machine. It is a cheap, fast and dead accurate way to pattern any compound curve — the same method works on tractor seats, boat cushions and car interiors.

### The pattern pieces

The shrink-wrap skin cut apart along the marked lines into flat pattern pieces — top, fronts and back, with the piping runs labelled.
The wrap is then cut off along the drawn seam lines, and what was a three-dimensional skin becomes a set of flat pattern pieces — the big top panel, the front sides, the back band — each labelled with its name, its piping runs and its balance marks. These get laid onto the vinyl and cut out with half an inch added on every edge for the seam allowance. That half inch is the whole trick: the pattern is the finished seam line, and the allowance is what the machine sews through.

### Sewing the cover

Sewing the cover on the industrial flat-bed — diamond-stitched top panel, plain sides, red piping caught in the seam.
The panels come together on the industrial flat-bed machine. The top is a double-diamond quilted vinyl with contrast stitching; the skirt is plain black vinyl; and the red piping is caught in the seam between them, following the line drawn on the shrink wrap all those steps ago. The balance marks earn their keep here — vinyl does not forgive a mis-aligned seam the way a loose-weave fabric might, so the panels are matched mark to mark as they feed through.

### The cover fitted

The finished cover fitted over the new foam — flat top, diamond stitching, red piping tracing the edge.
The sewn cover pulls over the new foam and the tension goes in evenly, working from the centre out so the diamond pattern sits square and the piping runs true along the top edge, before the cover is fixed off underneath to the original pan. This is the moment the shrink-wrap pattern proves itself: the cover fits the new shape like it grew there, with no excess to shrink out and no drum-tight flat spots.

### Back on the bike

Back on the bike — the flat profile completely changes the line of the machine.
Bolted back on, and the difference is immediate. The flat seat changes the whole line of the bike — leaner and lower-looking than the stepped original, in the custom style the owner was after.

### The detail up close

The detail that makes it — double-diamond stitching and red piping picking up the tank's pinstripe.
Up close, the details do the talking: the double-diamond stitch across the top, and the red piping tracing the seat's edge — chosen to pick up the red pinstripe on the Kawasaki's tank, so the seat looks like it belongs to this bike rather than just sitting on it.

### The finished bike

The finished bike — a one-off seat on a classic Kawasaki, ready for the road.
The finished machine. One seat pan, new foam, a shrink-wrap pattern and a session at the sewing machine — and a classic Kawasaki gets a one-off seat you cannot buy off a shelf.

### The methods behind this job

Every technique used here is set out in full in the book:

- [Foam Construction](https://www.learntoupholster.com/foam-construction)

- [Stripping the Old Work](https://www.learntoupholster.com/stripping-the-old-work)

- [Piping & bias strips](https://www.learntoupholster.com/piping-calculator)

- [Foam & cushion spec](https://www.learntoupholster.com/foam-cushion-calculator)



### Questions about this job

#### Can the shape of a motorbike seat be changed, or only the cover?

The shape can absolutely be changed — that is exactly what happened here. The foam is cut back and rebuilt to whatever profile the rider wants: flatter, lower, narrower at the nose, more support at the back. As long as the metal or plastic seat pan underneath is sound, it is reused with all its original fixings, so the reshaped seat bolts straight back onto the bike.

#### How do you make a pattern for a motorbike seat cover?

With shrink wrap. The shaped seat is wrapped tightly until the film forms a firm skin, the seam lines and balance marks are drawn on in marker, and the skin is cut off along those lines into flat pattern pieces. Each piece is laid on the vinyl and cut out with half an inch of seam allowance added on every edge. It is the standard trimmer's method for patterning any compound curve where no usable old cover exists.

#### What material should a motorbike seat be covered in?

Automotive-grade vinyl, not furnishing fabric. A bike seat lives outdoors in rain, sun and road grime, so the cover needs to be waterproof, UV-stable and hard-wearing — which is what marine and automotive vinyls are made for. On this seat, the top panel is a double-diamond quilted vinyl with contrast stitching and the sides are plain black vinyl, with vinyl-wrapped piping in the seams.

#### Do you keep the original seat pan and fittings?

Wherever possible, yes. The pan carries all the mounting points, hinges and catches that locate the seat on the frame, and those are usually the hardest parts to reproduce. On this Kawasaki the original pan was sound, so it was stripped, kept, and rebuilt with new foam — meaning the finished seat fits and fastens exactly as the factory one did.

### Have a piece like this?

Find a professional upholsterer near you — UK, US and worldwide — to bring your own chair, sofa or piece back to life.
