- A throw where the dog actually lies. Dogs are creatures of habit and will use the same spot. A washable sacrificial layer on that spot does more than any fabric choice.

- Arm caps. Old-fashioned, and they exist because arms wear out first.

### Test the sample before you commit

Get a decent-sized cutting, not a postage stamp, and do three things to it. Drag a key or a fingernail across it firmly and see if anything lifts. Put a few drops of water on it and see whether they sit or soak. Rub it hard with a cloth twenty times and see whether the surface changes.

Two minutes of that tells you more than any label. If you want to see how a cloth will actually look on your piece first, the fabric visualiser will show you before you buy, and our own fabric shop at Bodella will send samples.

### The honest summary

There is no dog-proof fabric, and anyone selling you one is selling you something. What there is, is a range that runs from "this will be ruined within a year" to "this will look fine for a decade with sensible care", and the distance between those two is mostly decided by whether the cloth has loops in it.

If somebody asked me for one answer with no further conversation: a mid-tone flecked polyester or performance weave, at least 40,000 Martindale, with zipped removable cushion covers and a throw on the dog's favourite end.

And if the dog is going to be on the sofa regardless — and it is — then choosing a cloth that survives it is a great deal more sensible than fighting about it for the next ten years.

### Common questions

#### What is the most hard-wearing upholstery fabric for dogs?

A tightly woven polyester, performance weave, microfibre or solution-dyed acrylic with a Martindale rating of at least 40,000 rubs. Solution-dyed acrylic is the toughest of the group and many types can be cleaned with dilute bleach without losing colour. Whatever the fibre, the weave must be flat with no loops, because loops are what claws destroy.

#### Is bouclé a bad choice with pets?

Yes, it is close to the worst choice available. Bouclé is constructed entirely from loops, and a claw that catches a loop pulls it into a run that cannot be repaired invisibly. The same applies to any heavily looped or nubby weave. Run a fingernail firmly across a sample: if anything lifts or catches, it will not survive a dog or a cat.

#### Is leather good for dog owners?

It is a trade-off rather than an upgrade. Hair does not embed in leather and wipes off, spills wipe off and it holds no smell, which is a real daily advantage with a shedding breed. Against that, claws scratch it and there is no weave to protect the surface. Pigmented or corrected-grain leather hides scratching best and can be recoloured; aniline records everything; bonded and faux leather should be avoided entirely, because a punctured coating goes on to peel.

#### What colour sofa hides dog hair best?

A mid-tone in roughly the colour of your dog, with some tonal variation in the weave. Flecks, tweeds and heathered cloths disguise hair and small marks far better than flat solid colours. Very dark fabrics show light hair and dust, very pale fabrics show everything else, and plain pale grey is the least forgiving cloth in common use.

## Why do two upholsterers quote such different prices? — https://www.learntoupholster.com/blog/why-do-upholstery-quotes-differ

### Why is one reupholstery quote so much higher than another?

Because the two quotes are almost never for the same job. The biggest single cause is that one is a recover — a new cover fitted over the existing fillings — and the other is a full reupholster, stripped to the frame and rebuilt. Both get called reupholstery and the difference in work can be double or more. After that come fabric quantity and grade, whether the foam, webbing and springs are being renewed, frame repairs, VAT registration, collection and delivery, and the difference between a workshop with premises and a sole trader working from home. A cheap quote usually means less work, not a better deal.

Anybody who gets three quotes for the same sofa will get three very different numbers, and it unsettles people. It looks like somebody must be trying it on.

Usually nobody is. The quotes differ because the jobs differ, and the customer has no way of seeing that from three figures on three emails. So here is what is actually varying underneath, and the questions that make the numbers comparable.

### The big one: recover or reupholster?

These are two genuinely different jobs and the trade uses both words loosely, which is where most of the confusion comes from.

A recover means taking the old cover off and fitting a new one over the fillings that are already there. The foam stays, the webbing stays, the springs stay. It is a legitimate job on a piece that is structurally sound and simply looks tired.

A full reupholster means stripping the piece back to the bare frame, repairing the frame, renewing webbing and springs, replacing fillings, and building it back up. It is the difference between painting a house and rebuilding the walls.

One can easily be double the other, and both will be described to you as "reupholstering the sofa". If you ask nothing else, ask this.

### What is being replaced underneath

Once you know which job you are being quoted for, the next question is what specifically is being renewed. In rough order of cost:

- Foam and fillings. New foam of a decent density is not cheap, and the density specified makes a real difference to both price and how the finished piece feels. A quote that reuses tired foam under a beautiful new cover will look wonderful and feel exactly as it did before.

- Webbing. Renewing elastic or jute webbing means getting into the underside or lifting the deck. Not enormous, but not nothing.

- Springs. Re-tying traditional springs is hours of skilled work. Replacing sinuous springs needs the right gauge and clips.

- Frame repairs. Re-gluing joints, new corner blocks, a replacement rail. Only possible once the piece is stripped, which is why it often appears as a variation rather than in the original quote.

If one quote is markedly cheaper, this list is usually where the difference lives.

### Fabric — and whether it is even included

Some upholsterers quote labour only and expect you to supply cloth. Some quote inclusive of a fabric at a stated price per metre. Comparing one of each is meaningless.

What you need from each quote is the same three numbers: how many metres, at what price per metre, and is it in the figure or not.

Metreage itself varies legitimately. A patterned cloth needs more than a plain because panels have to be cut to match the repeat, and a one-way cloth such as velvet cannot be turned or nested efficiently. An upholsterer quoting on a plain and another quoting on your chosen patterned fabric will differ by metres, not centimetres. Our yardage calculator will give you a baseline figure to sanity-check against.

### Two workshops, two cost bases

A sole trader working from a home workshop with no staff has a very different overhead to a firm with commercial premises, employees, vans, showroom and public liability cover across the lot. Neither is doing anything wrong. They simply cannot charge the same and both survive.

What you get for the higher overhead is usually capacity, insurance, a proper collection and delivery service and somebody answering the phone. What you get for the lower one is often the owner's own hands on your chair for the whole job. Both are legitimate purchases. Decide which you are buying.

### VAT, which is invisible and worth 20%

An upholsterer registered for VAT has to add it. One trading below the threshold does not. That is a fifth of the price difference on identical work, with no difference whatsoever in what you receive.

It is not a trick and neither party is doing anything improper — but it explains a chunk of variance that otherwise looks inexplicable. Ask whether the figure includes VAT.

### The rest of it

- Collection and delivery. Two people and a van for half a day, sometimes twice. Frequently excluded from the cheaper quote.

- Fixed price or estimate. On an antique nobody knows what is inside until it is stripped. An honest estimate says so and states the basis for any variation. A fixed price on an unknown piece is either optimistic or padded.

- Timescale. A four-week turnaround and a nine-month waiting list are different products.

- Guarantee. Ask what is covered and for how long.

### When a quote is too cheap

Some warning signs, none of which are conclusive alone.

- They quoted without seeing the piece, from a photograph, with no questions about what is underneath.

- The quote is a single figure with no breakdown of labour, fabric and materials.

- Nobody mentioned fire regulations. This is the one I would weigh most heavily. Reupholstery work in the UK carries real obligations around fire safety, and any competent upholsterer will raise it unprompted — particularly if you are supplying your own fabric, because that determines whether an interliner is needed. If it never comes up, ask why. Our fire safety checker will tell you what should apply to your piece.

- Large deposit, cash preferred, no written specification.

### The five questions that make quotes comparable

Send these to everyone quoting, in writing, and the numbers become readable:

- Is this a recover or a full reupholster?

- What exactly is being replaced — foam, webbing, springs, frame repairs?

- Is fabric included? How many metres, at what price per metre?

- Does the price include collection, delivery and VAT?

- Is it a fixed price or an estimate, and what happens if you find something once it is stripped?

Any upholsterer worth using will answer all five without hesitation, because they already know the answers. The quality of the answers tells you more than the figure does.

### And when a quote is too expensive

Expensive is not automatically better, and I would be doing you no favours pretending otherwise. If the higher quote cannot explain itself in terms of specific additional work — more replaced, better fillings, frame repairs included, a more complex fabric — then it is just a higher price.

What you are looking for is not the cheapest or the dearest. It is the one where the answers to those five questions match the number, and where the person answering clearly understood the piece in front of them.

### Why the cheapest often costs more

The thing that makes reupholstery expensive is labour, and the great majority of that labour is in stripping the piece and building it back up. If a job is done cheaply and the fillings underneath are left as they were, that labour still gets spent — it simply gets spent again in a few years when the seat collapses under a cover that is still perfectly good.

Doing it once properly is very often cheaper than doing it twice, which is an unsatisfying thing to be told when you are looking at two numbers and one of them is smaller. But it is the honest answer, and it is why the question worth asking is never "how much" on its own. It is "how much, for what".

### Common questions

#### What is the difference between recovering and reupholstering?

Recovering means fitting a new cover over the existing fillings, springs and webbing. Reupholstering means stripping the piece back to the bare frame and rebuilding it — new webbing, springs re-tied or replaced, new fillings, frame repairs. The work involved can differ by a factor of two or more, yet both jobs are commonly described as reupholstery, which is the single biggest reason quotes vary so widely.

#### Should I always get three quotes for reupholstery?

Getting more than one is sensible, but only if you give every upholsterer the same brief and ask each of them the same questions — recover or full reupholster, what is being replaced underneath, whether fabric is included and at what metreage and price, whether collection, delivery and VAT are in the figure, and whether it is fixed or an estimate. Three numbers for three different jobs tell you nothing.

#### Is a cheap reupholstery quote a bad sign?

Not necessarily, but it usually means less work rather than better value — most often a recover rather than a full rebuild, or reusing the existing foam and webbing. Warning signs worth taking seriously are quoting from a photograph without inspecting the piece, a single figure with no breakdown, and no mention of fire safety obligations, which any competent upholsterer raises unprompted.

#### Why does VAT make such a difference to upholstery quotes?

An upholsterer registered for VAT must add it to the bill, while one trading below the registration threshold does not. That is a 20% difference on identical work with no difference in what you receive. It is entirely legitimate on both sides, and it explains a good deal of variance that otherwise looks inexplicable, so it is always worth asking whether a quoted figure includes VAT.

## Why does leather peel? — https://www.learntoupholster.com/blog/why-does-leather-peel

### Why is my leather sofa peeling?

Because it almost certainly is not leather. Genuine leather does not peel — it fades, softens, scuffs and eventually cracks, but it does not shed flakes from its surface. Peeling in sheets or flakes is the signature failure of bonded leather and of polyurethane-coated faux leather, where a thin plastic skin is separating from the backing underneath. There is one exception: heavily pigmented corrected-grain leather can lose its surface finish at high-wear points, which looks like peeling but leaves sound leather beneath and can be recoloured. Bonded and PU cannot be repaired. They can only be re-covered.

This is the single most common question I get from the public, and almost every answer online gets it wrong. People ring up furious with leather as a material, convinced they have been sold a dud hide. They have not. In nine cases out of ten they were never sold leather at all.

So it is worth being precise about what is actually happening on that sofa arm.

### Leather does not peel. Plastic does.

A hide is a solid material all the way through. Colour is either dyed into it or sits on it as a thin pigment layer, but the substance beneath is one continuous thing. There is no separate skin to come away, because there is no separate skin.

What fails on a hide is different, and it looks different. Real leather dries out, loses suppleness, goes shiny where bodies rub it, fades in sunlight, and if it is left dry for long enough it cracks — splits that open into the material rather than lifting off it. Wear on genuine leather goes inward. Peeling goes outward.

When you can pick at an edge with a fingernail and lift a flake away, revealing a different-coloured fabric or fibrous mat underneath, you are looking at a coating that has stopped sticking to its backing. That is a manufactured laminate failing, and it is a completely different problem with a completely different answer.

### The six things sold as "leather"

Part of the confusion is deliberate. The retail trade uses a set of terms that sound reassuring and mean very little. Here is what is actually on the shop floor, roughly best to worst for longevity.

- Full-grain. The complete outer surface of the hide, nothing sanded away. Toughest fibre structure there is. Marks and darkens with use into a patina. Will not peel. Will outlive you if it is fed occasionally.

- Top-grain. The grain surface lightly sanded to even out blemishes, then finished. The great majority of good upholstery leather. Excellent life. Will not peel.

- Corrected-grain or pigmented. Heavily sanded, an artificial grain embossed in, then a substantial pigment and topcoat sprayed over. Real leather underneath, but the finish is doing the visual work. This one can flake at high-wear points — and it is the exception that makes this whole question confusing. More on it below.

- Split. The lower layer of a hide after the grain has been taken off. No grain structure, so it is finished, embossed or brushed into suede. Weaker, and any applied finish sits on a fibrous surface with less to grip.

- Bonded leather. Leather offcuts shredded into fibre, mixed with adhesive, spread onto a fabric or paper backing, and topped with a polyurethane layer embossed to look like grain. Leather content is often somewhere around a tenth to a fifth of the material. It is chipboard, in leather terms. This is the classic peeler.

- Faux leather. Polyurethane or PVC coating on a woven or knitted textile backing. Sold as leatherette, pleather, PU, or lately as vegan leather. No hide involved at any point. The other classic peeler.

Watch for the phrase genuine leather on a swing tag. It sounds like a guarantee and functions as the opposite — it is the lowest grade term in common use, and it very often means a finished split. It tells you an animal was involved. It tells you nothing about how long the thing will last.

### How to tell what you have got

You can usually settle this in about a minute, without any specialist kit.

- Look at a cut edge. Under a cushion, at a seam, on the underside of a skirt. Real leather is the same material through its thickness, with a slightly fibrous, suede-like reverse. Bonded and faux show a clear sandwich: a coloured skin sitting on an obviously different backing, often a woven or knitted cloth.

- Look at where it is failing. Peeling that starts at the seat front, the arm tops and the head area — precisely where bodies press and rub — and lifts in flakes is coating failure. Wear on real leather in those same places goes shiny and soft first.

- Press it. Real leather warms to the hand quickly and creases into fine irregular lines that stay. Coated materials feel cooler for longer and fold in more uniform, springier creases.

- Check the grain pattern. Embossed grain repeats. If you can find the same distinctive mark twice on different panels, it came off a roller, not an animal.

- Smell it. Crude, but leather smells like leather and PU smells faintly of plastic. Less reliable on old pieces that have absorbed a room's worth of other smells.

### Why the coating lets go

Polyurethane fails by hydrolysis. Moisture in ordinary household air slowly breaks down the polymer's chemical bonds, and it does so on a timetable that has very little to do with how carefully you treat the sofa. Warm, humid rooms accelerate it. The material is degrading from the day it is made, and eventually the layer loses both its integrity and its grip on the backing.

On bonded leather there is a second weakness. The adhesive holding the fibre mat to its backing is doing structural work it is not really built for, and every time somebody sits down, that laminate flexes. Flex a glued sandwich a few thousand times and it delaminates.

Then the ordinary business of being furniture speeds it all up:

- Body oils and sweat. The head rest and arm tops go first on almost every piece, and it is not a coincidence — those are the contact points.

- Sunlight and heat. A sofa against a radiator or in a bay window ages measurably faster at that end. I have seen pieces where you can read the sun's path across the back cushions.

- The wrong cleaners. Baby wipes are the great destroyer. The surfactants in them strip finish, and people use them precisely because they are gentle on skin. Solvent cleaners and silicone polishes do their own damage.

In the workshop, bonded and PU pieces commonly start shedding somewhere between their second and fifth year. That is trade observation rather than a published figure, but it is remarkably consistent — and it is a fraction of what people expect when they buy something described as leather.

### The exception: pigmented leather losing its finish

Here is where honest confusion is possible, because this genuinely is leather and it genuinely does flake.

Corrected-grain pigmented leather carries a thick sprayed finish. At the points that take the most abrasion — seat front edge, arm tops, the outer third of a seat cushion — that finish can crack and lift, leaving pale patches with ragged edges. It looks like peeling. Customers describe it as peeling.

The difference is what is underneath. Lift a flake of bonded leather and you find fabric backing. Lift a flake of failed pigment and you find leather — sound, if a different colour to the surface.

That distinction decides everything, because one of these is repairable and the other is not.

### What can be repaired, honestly

I would rather tell someone the truth on the phone than take a deposit for work that will not hold.

- Pigmented leather with finish loss: repairable. A leather refinishing specialist can clean back, fill, recolour and seal, and a good job lasts years. Worth doing on a decent frame.

- Real leather that is dry, faded or lightly cracked: often improves a great deal with proper feeding and conditioning. Cracks that have not split right through can be stabilised.

- Real leather split through, or torn: panel replacement. An upholsterer can cut and fit a new panel, though matching an aged hide is genuinely difficult and it is usually better to replace a whole section than to patch.

- Bonded leather, peeling: not repairable. Nothing will bond reliably to a surface that is actively delaminating. Vinyl paints and repair kits will look acceptable for a few months and then lift along with everything else. Anyone promising otherwise is selling you a kit.

- Faux leather, peeling: the same answer. Re-cover or replace.

The good news is that re-covering is very often worth it. If the frame is solid hardwood and the suspension is sound — which on a decent piece it usually is, even when the covering has failed early — then the expensive, hard-to-replace part of that sofa is still perfectly good. You are replacing the skin, not the animal.

### Making real leather last

If you do have genuine leather, it wants very little, but it does want that little consistently.

- Keep it out of direct sun and away from radiators. Heat and UV do more damage than use does.

- Dust it and wipe it with a barely damp cloth. Nothing else, most of the time.

- Feed it once or twice a year with a proper leather conditioner suited to the finish. Aniline and pigmented leathers want different products — ask before you buy.

- Never use baby wipes, household cleaning sprays, solvent, or anything containing silicone.

- Deal with spills immediately by blotting, not rubbing.

Do that and a good hide will look better at twenty years than it did at one.

### What I tell people on the phone

When somebody rings about a peeling sofa, the first question is not what it costs. It is: can you go and pick at a flake and tell me what is underneath?

If it is fabric backing, I explain that they have bonded or faux leather, that nothing can be done to repair it, and that their choice is re-cover or replace. Most people are relieved to be given a straight answer, even a disappointing one — they have usually been told by three other people that a repair kit will sort it.

If it is leather underneath, I send them to a refinishing specialist, because that is a proper trade in its own right and they will do a better job of it than I will.

And if the frame is good and they want it re-covered, then we are having a much more enjoyable conversation about hides.

### Common questions

#### Can peeling leather be repaired?

Only if it is real leather losing its surface finish, in which case a leather refinishing specialist can recolour and reseal it. If the flakes lift to reveal a fabric backing, it is bonded or faux leather and no repair will hold, because nothing bonds reliably to a delaminating surface. Repair kits on bonded leather look acceptable for a few months and then lift with everything else.

#### Is bonded leather real leather?

Only partly. It is made from shredded leather offcuts mixed with adhesive, spread on a fabric or paper backing and topped with an embossed polyurethane layer. Actual leather content is often around a tenth to a fifth of the material. It is legally describable as containing leather, but it behaves like a plastic laminate, not like a hide.

#### How long should a leather sofa last?

Good top-grain or full-grain leather on a sound frame should last decades and improve in appearance as it goes. Bonded and polyurethane faux leather commonly begin shedding within two to five years. If a sofa described as leather starts peeling early, the material is the reason, not the way it was treated.

#### Why is my sofa peeling only on the arms and headrest?

Because those are the contact points. Body oils, sweat and constant abrasion break down a surface coating fastest exactly where people touch it. On coated materials this shows as flaking; on genuine leather the same areas simply go shiny and soft first. The pattern of failure is itself a clue to which material you have.

## Why does velvet go patchy? — https://www.learntoupholster.com/blog/why-does-velvet-go-patchy

### Why does my velvet sofa look patchy?

Because velvet is a pile fabric, and pile reflects light differently depending on which way it is lying. Press it, sit on it, or stroke it the wrong way and that patch reflects light differently to the cloth around it, so it reads as a lighter or darker mark. It is called shading or pressure marking, it is inherent to the way velvet is made, and it is not a fault. Whether it comes out again depends almost entirely on the fibre: cotton and polyester velvets usually recover with steam and brushing, while viscose velvet very often does not. If a supplier tells you their velvet will never mark, they are either selling polyester or not telling the truth.

Velvet is the fabric that generates more complaints than any other, and almost none of them are faults. It is also the fabric people fall in love with hardest, which is why the disappointment stings when the first visitor gets up and leaves a shadow across the seat.

So it is worth explaining what is actually happening, because once you understand it you can either choose a velvet that suits how you live, or stop worrying about it.

### Velvet is a pile fabric, and that is the whole story

Most cloth is flat. The surface you see is the weave itself, and it looks the same from wherever you stand.

Velvet is not flat. It has a dense forest of short fibre ends standing up from a woven backing, and those ends behave like millions of tiny mirrors. When they all lean the same way, light bounces off them uniformly and you get that deep, even lustre. When a patch of them gets pushed over in a different direction, that patch throws light somewhere else and reads as a different shade.

Nothing has stained. Nothing has faded. Nothing has worn. The fibres are simply lying at a different angle to their neighbours.

Move round the room and the mark will often change or disappear entirely, which is the giveaway. A stain looks like a stain from every angle. Shading does not.

### The word velvet tells you almost nothing

This is where most of the trouble starts. Velvet describes a construction, not a material — and the fibre it is made from matters far more than the word on the label.

- Cotton velvet. Traditional, matt rather than glossy, handsome. Marks readily but usually recovers with steam and brushing. Good on period pieces.

- Linen velvet. Similar behaviour, with a drier, more textured handle. Creases as linen does.

- Mohair velvet. The connoisseur's choice and priced accordingly. Angora goat fibre — springy, resilient, extraordinarily hard-wearing, and it resists crushing better than anything else. Original Victorian and Edwardian pieces were often covered in it and a great many are still going.

- Silk velvet. Beautiful, fragile, and honestly not an upholstery cloth for anything that gets sat on daily.

- Viscose velvet. Often sold on its glorious shine and its price. It is regenerated cellulose, it loses a great deal of its strength when damp, and its pile does not spring back. This is the one that marks permanently. Also the one most often behind a furious phone call.

- Polyester velvet. Frequently sold as performance velvet. Far less glamorous to a purist, and by a wide margin the most forgiving in a family house. Resists crushing, tolerates cleaning, and recovers well.

Two near relatives worth knowing, because they get called velvet in shops. Velveteen has a much shorter pile made from the weft rather than a separate warp, so it is flatter and marks less. Velour is knitted rather than woven, which makes it stretchy — a different animal entirely, and it behaves differently under tension on a frame.

### Pile direction, and why your upholsterer keeps going on about it

Run your hand over velvet one way and it feels smooth. Run it the other way and it feels like it is resisting slightly, and the colour shifts. That is the pile direction, and deciding it is one of the first things done in the workshop before a single panel is cut.

The convention in this country is pile running down — smooth when you stroke from the top of the piece towards the floor, and from the back of a seat towards the front edge. Pile down gives a lighter, more lustrous look, sheds dust rather than collecting it, and wears more evenly because the pile is being pushed the way it already wants to lie.

Pile running up gives a deeper, richer, darker colour. It is a legitimate choice and some designers prefer it, particularly on a statement chair. It will show marks more and it will collect more dust.

What matters far more than which one you choose is that every panel runs the same way. One panel cut upside down on an otherwise perfect job will read as a different colour under the window, and there is no fixing it short of recutting. It is the single most common error on velvet in workshops that do not work with it often.

If you are buying velvet and having it made up elsewhere, ask outright which way the pile will run and whether every panel will match. A workshop that answers immediately and without hedging has done this before.

### Velvet costs you more fabric, before anyone has bought anything

Because every panel has to run the same way, velvet is a one-way cloth. On a plain fabric an upholsterer can turn a panel ninety degrees or flip it end to end to squeeze it out of an awkward gap in the cutting plan. On velvet none of that is available.

In practice this behaves much like a pattern repeat: expect to allow more cloth than a plain fabric of the same width for the same piece, and take the estimate from someone who knows it is velvet. Getting a quantity from a plain-fabric rule of thumb and then buying velvet is a reliable way to end up half a metre short with a discontinued dye lot.

Our fabric yardage calculator will get you a starting figure, but tell your upholsterer it is velvet before they order.

### Pressure marks: what comes out and what does not

Three different things get lumped together under "marking", and they have different outcomes.

- Shading. Broad soft variations in tone across a panel, changing as you move around the room. Entirely normal, present from day one on most velvets, and part of the character. Nothing to fix.

- Pressure marks. Defined patches where somebody has sat, knelt or set something down. On cotton, linen, mohair and polyester these usually lift with gentle steam and brushing. On viscose they very often do not.

- Watermarking. Wavy, cloudy patterns that appear after the pile gets damp — sometimes from cleaning, sometimes just from a humid room or a wet coat laid over an arm. On viscose this is generally permanent. It is why you should never wet-clean a viscose velvet.

To lift an ordinary pressure mark: hold a steamer or steam iron above the surface without touching it, let the steam relax the pile, then brush gently in the pile direction with a soft clothes brush and let it dry undisturbed. Patience works better than pressure. Never press an iron onto velvet — it will flatten the pile permanently and that is a mark nothing removes.

### Living with it

None of this makes velvet a bad choice. It makes it a choice that rewards knowing what you are buying.

- Brush the piece occasionally with a soft brush, always in the pile direction.

- Vacuum with an upholstery brush head on low suction, again in the pile direction.

- Rotate and turn loose cushions so wear and marking spread evenly.

- Blot spills immediately, never rub — rubbing distorts the pile and leaves a mark worse than the spill.

- Keep viscose velvet away from anything damp, and get any real cleaning done by a specialist who has been told what fibre it is.

- Check the Martindale rating on the spec sheet, and do not put a light-domestic velvet on the sofa the whole family uses.

### What I tell people choosing velvet

I ask two questions. Who sits on it, and can you live with marks?

If the answer is a formal sitting room used twice a week and yes, then almost any velvet will make you happy, and a cotton or mohair one will look glorious for decades.

If the answer is two children, a dog and every evening, then I steer firmly towards a good polyester performance velvet. It will not have quite the depth of a cotton velvet under a lamp. It will also still look like a sofa in five years, which matters more.

And if somebody has fallen in love with a viscose velvet, I tell them plainly what it will do, put it in writing on the quote, and then cover the piece in it if they still want it. It is their sofa. What is not acceptable is them finding out afterwards.

### Common questions

#### Are pressure marks in velvet a fault?

No. Shading and pressure marking are inherent to pile fabric and are specifically excluded from most fabric warranties. The pile fibres are lying at a different angle and reflecting light differently, which is how velvet works. A genuine fault would be something like a pile that pulls out, an uneven backing, or a flaw running through the weave.

#### Can pressure marks be removed from velvet?

Usually on cotton, linen, mohair and polyester velvet. Hold a steamer above the surface without touching it, brush gently in the pile direction with a soft brush, and let it dry undisturbed. Viscose velvet very often will not recover, and any watermarking on viscose is generally permanent, which is why it should never be wet-cleaned.

#### Which velvet is the most hard-wearing?

Mohair velvet, comfortably, and it is priced to match — Victorian and Edwardian pieces covered in it are frequently still in service. For an everyday budget, a good polyester performance velvet is the practical answer: it resists crushing, recovers from marks and tolerates cleaning. Check the Martindale rating rather than trusting the description.

#### Does velvet need more fabric than plain cloth?

Yes. Because the pile must run the same way on every panel, velvet is a one-way cloth and panels cannot be turned or flipped to fit the cutting plan efficiently. Allow extra in much the same way you would for a pattern repeat, and always tell whoever is estimating that the fabric is velvet before the order goes in.

## Why has my sofa gone saggy in the middle? — https://www.learntoupholster.com/blog/why-has-my-sofa-gone-saggy

### Why does my sofa sag in the middle?

Because something underneath the cushions has given way, and in most cases it is not the cushions themselves. There are only three real suspects: the seat foam has compressed and stopped springing back, the suspension underneath has failed — stretched elastic webbing, a detached or broken sinuous spring, or perished jute webbing on an older piece — or the frame itself is flexing, usually because a long seat rail has no support in the middle. You can tell which it is in about two minutes with the cushions off, and the answer decides whether this is a cheap fix or a conversation about whether the sofa is worth keeping.

Almost everyone diagnoses this wrongly, and understandably so. The cushion is the bit you sit on, the cushion is the bit that feels wrong, so the cushion must be the problem. New cushions get ordered, they go in, and six weeks later it feels exactly the same.

That is because the cushion was sitting on something that had already failed. Put a new cushion on a collapsed deck and you have simply given the collapse a nicer covering.

### Start by taking the cushions off

Everything follows from this. Strip the seat cushions off entirely and look at what they were sitting on — the deck, in trade terms.

Then press down firmly on the deck with the flat of your hand, working across the whole width. What you are feeling for is whether it supports your hand evenly or whether there is a hollow.

- The deck feels firm and even everywhere. The cushions are the problem, and that is the good news. Foam replacement, and you are done.

- The deck sinks in the middle, or your hand meets a hollow. The suspension has gone. This is the most common answer.

- The deck feels reasonable but the whole seat moves or the front rail dips when you press. The frame is flexing, and that is the serious one.

Three suspects, and a two-minute test that narrows it down. Now for what each one actually means.

### Suspect one: the cushion foam has given up

Foam does not wear out so much as it takes a set. Every time you sit down, the cell structure is compressed; over years it loses the ability to push back to its original height. The trade term is compression set, and it is why a cushion can look full when you lift it out and feel like nothing when you sit on it.

The tell is that the sagging follows people. The seat somebody always uses is dead, the seat nobody uses is fine, and the cushions are visibly different heights when you stand them side by side.

This is the cheapest problem you can have. New foam of the right density, wrapped properly, transforms a sofa — and if the covers are sound, an upholsterer can often do it without touching the covering at all. Our foam and cushion spec tool will tell you what density you should be asking for, which is worth knowing before you ring anyone, because the single most common reason a foam replacement disappoints is that somebody fitted the cheap grade.

### Suspect two: the suspension has failed

This is what is under the deck, holding everything up, and there are three kinds depending on how old and how good the sofa is.

Elastic webbing — wide black rubberised straps stretched across the frame, standard on most modern sofas. It is designed to stretch, which is also its weakness: after years under load it stops recovering and hangs slack. It also fails at its fixings, where staples or clips pull out of the rail. A slack strap in the middle of a run gives you exactly the dip you are feeling.

Sinuous springs — also called zig-zag or serpentine, the S-shaped steel wires running front to back under the deck. They fail in two ways: the clip holding one end lets go of the frame, or the wire itself snaps. Both give a sudden, localised collapse rather than a gradual sag, and there is often a noise involved — a twang or a clunk when somebody sits down. If your sofa developed a dip overnight rather than over years, this is almost certainly why.

Coil springs on jute webbing — traditional construction, older or better pieces. The springs themselves rarely fail, but the jute webbing carrying them perishes, stretches or tears at the tacks, and the twine tying the spring tops together rots. When it goes, the whole spring unit drops.

Getting at any of these means turning the sofa over and taking off the black cloth underneath, the cambric or dust cover. That is a legitimate thing to do yourself just to look — it is stapled on and it goes back with a staple gun.

If you are only investigating, cut the dust cover along one edge rather than tearing it off. It goes back with a dozen staples and nobody will ever see it.

### Suspect three: the frame

This is the one that decides whether the sofa has a future.

The middle of a long seat is simply the furthest point from anything holding it up. On a properly built sofa there is a centre rail, or a centre leg, or both, carrying the load across the span. On a cheaply built one there often is not, and the front rail is a length of softwood expected to bridge two metres on its own. Over years, under people, it bows.

The tells are a front edge that is visibly lower in the middle than at the ends when you sight along it, a seat that moves or creaks as a whole when you sit, and a frame that flexes when you push down hard on the deck near the front.

Sometimes this is genuinely repairable — a new centre leg, a reinforcing rail, re-gluing a joint that has opened. Our chapter on frame repair and joint reinforcement covers what is possible. But it means stripping the sofa back to get at it, and on a stapled softwood frame you have to ask honestly whether it is worth doing.

### The plywood board, and why I keep being asked about it

The advice you will find everywhere is to slide a sheet of plywood or a "sofa saver" board under the cushions. It is worth being straight about what that does.

It works, in the sense that the sagging stops. It stops because you have taken the suspension out of the equation entirely and are now sitting on a board. The seat becomes flat and hard, the cushion foam is being compressed against an unyielding surface rather than a sprung one, so it breaks down faster, and the load that was spread across the webbing is now concentrated on the frame rails at each end.

As a stopgap for a few weeks before a proper repair, or on a piece you are running to the end of its life deliberately, it is a perfectly reasonable thing to do. As a permanent answer it is masking the fault and quietly making the next repair bigger. Just know which one you are choosing.

### So is it worth fixing?

Roughly, in ascending order of trouble:

- Foam only. Straightforward and inexpensive, often done without disturbing the covers. Almost always worth it.

- Elastic webbing. Straightforward for an upholsterer, needs the dust cover off and sometimes the deck lifted. Worth it on any decent sofa.

- Sinuous springs. More work, needs the right gauge spring and clips, but a proper repair that lasts. Worth it on a good frame.

- Traditional springs and jute webbing. A real job — but pieces built this way are usually worth the effort, because a frame from that era is generally hardwood and jointed rather than stapled.

- Frame. Depends entirely on what the frame is. Hardwood and jointed, fix it. Softwood, stapled, no centre rail, and already bowed — that sofa is telling you something.

The decision almost always comes down to the frame rather than the price of the repair, which is why an upholsterer will want to look underneath before quoting. If you want a figure to think with in the meantime, the cost estimator will give you a range.

### What I say on the phone

Take the cushions off, press the middle of the deck, and tell me whether your hand goes down.

If it does not, we are talking about foam and it is a good day. If it does, we are talking about what is underneath and I need to see it. And if you can sight along the front edge and tell me it dips in the middle, I will want to know how old the sofa is and what it cost, because the answer to that decides everything else.

Nobody enjoys being told a three-year-old sofa is not worth repairing. But it is a better conversation than taking somebody's money to put new foam on a collapsed frame.

### Common questions

#### Can a sagging sofa be fixed without reupholstering it?

Very often, yes. If the cushion foam has compressed, it can usually be replaced without touching the covers at all. If the elastic webbing or springs underneath have failed, an upholsterer works through the dust cover on the underside and the covering generally stays in place. Full reupholstery is only needed when the frame itself has to be reached.

#### Is putting plywood under sofa cushions a good idea?

As a short-term stopgap, it is reasonable. As a permanent fix it is not, because it removes the suspension from the equation entirely — you end up sitting on a board, the cushion foam breaks down faster against a hard flat surface, and the load transfers onto the frame rails. It hides the fault rather than fixing it, and it usually makes the eventual repair bigger.

#### Why does my sofa sag in the middle but not at the ends?

Because the middle of a seat is the furthest point from anything supporting it. The ends sit close to the arm frames and the legs; the middle of a long span is carried only by the webbing or springs and, on a well-built sofa, a centre rail or centre leg. Cheaper sofas frequently have no centre support at all, so the middle is where deflection shows first.

#### My sofa suddenly dipped rather than sagging gradually — what does that mean?

A sudden collapse, especially with a twang or a clunk when somebody sits down, usually means a sinuous spring has snapped or a spring clip has come away from the frame. Gradual sagging over years points to foam compression or elastic webbing losing its stretch. The difference in how it happened is a genuine diagnostic clue.

## Why is my sofa fabric bobbling? — https://www.learntoupholster.com/blog/why-is-my-sofa-fabric-bobbling

### Why does my sofa fabric bobble?

Because short loose fibres in the yarn are working their way to the surface, tangling into little balls under friction, and then being held there by the longer fibres they are still attached to. It is called pilling, it is a property of how the yarn was spun rather than a sign of misuse or poor cleaning, and on most fabrics it stops once the loose fibre has been used up — typically within the first few months. Blended fabrics are the worst offenders, because a strong fibre anchors the pills formed by a weaker one instead of letting them drop off. The fix is a fabric shaver, and the mistake is pulling them off by hand.

Everybody thinks bobbling means the fabric is wearing out. It usually means almost the opposite — the fabric is shedding the loose material it was made with, and once that is gone it settles down.

Worth understanding properly, though, because there is a version of this that is a fault, and knowing the difference is the difference between reaching for a five-pound gadget and making a complaint.

### What a pill actually is

Most upholstery yarn is spun from staple fibre — short lengths, a few centimetres each, twisted together into a thread. However well it is spun, some fibre ends sit near the surface rather than being locked into the twist.

Rub that surface and three things happen in order. The loose ends work their way out. They tangle with each other into a small ball. And then — this is the part that matters — that ball stays put, because it is still anchored by fibres that run back into the yarn.

So a pill is not fabric coming apart. It is fabric tidying itself up badly.

### Why blends are the worst

This is the bit that explains most real-world pilling and almost nobody mentions it.

Pure wool pills readily — but wool fibres are relatively weak in that situation, so the pills break off and fall away on their own. You may barely notice.

Put that same wool in a blend with polyester and the picture changes completely. The polyester is far stronger, it does not break, and it holds the pill on the surface indefinitely. You now have permanent bobbles made largely of wool, anchored by polyester that will not let go.

Which is why a poly-cotton or poly-wool blend often bobbles far more visibly than either fibre would alone. The blend was chosen to combine the strengths of both. It also combined a weakness neither had by itself.

### Which fabrics pill, roughly

- Worst: loosely spun staple blends — poly-cotton, poly-wool, acrylic mixes, and cheaply spun polyester staple.

- Moderate: pure wool, pure cotton, chenille. They pill, but the pills tend to shed.

- Least: filament yarns, where the fibre runs continuously through the thread rather than being spun from short lengths. Microfibre, most performance polyesters and solution-dyed acrylics come into this group. There are simply no loose ends to migrate.

- Effectively none: leather, vinyl, and tightly woven flat filament cloths.

Twist matters too. A tightly spun, tightly woven cloth holds its fibre ends in. A soft, loosely spun yarn — which is exactly what gives a fabric that lovely soft handle in the showroom — lets them out.

### Where it shows, and why there

Seat fronts, arm tops, headrests and the outer third of seat cushions. The same contact points as every other upholstery problem, because pilling needs friction and that is where friction happens.

Clothing plays a bigger part than people expect. Denim, knitwear and fleece are abrasive, and they also contribute their own loose fibre into the mix. A sofa used mostly by somebody in a jumper will bobble faster than one used by somebody in a shirt, all else being equal.

### Does it stop?

On a decent fabric, yes. There is a finite quantity of loose fibre in the cloth, and once it has migrated out and been removed, the surface stabilises. Expect the worst of it in the first three to six months, then a marked decline.

If it is still producing new pills a year in, at the same rate, that is a different problem. That points to a yarn that is genuinely shedding rather than settling, and it is worth taking up with whoever supplied the fabric.

### How to get rid of them

One tool, and it costs very little.

A battery fabric shaver. A rotating blade behind a mesh guard that cuts the pills off flush without touching the cloth. It is the right answer and it is what upholsterers and dry cleaners use.

Technique, because people do get this wrong:

- Work on a flat, supported surface — lay the cushion down rather than shaving it in place on a curved arm.

- Light pressure. Let the blade do it. Pressing the guard into the weave is how you cut the fabric itself.

- Short overlapping passes in one direction, not scrubbing back and forth.

- Empty the collector often; a full one stops cutting cleanly.

- Vacuum afterwards.

And the things not to do:

- Do not pull them off by hand. The pill is anchored to fibres running into the yarn. Pulling it drags those out too, and you are now removing cloth rather than surplus.

- Do not use a razor blade or a disposable razor. It works right up until it takes a slice out of the weave, and on a pile fabric it will shave the pile flat.

- Do not use a razor on velvet, chenille or anything with a pile at all. A shaver on its highest guard setting, very lightly, or leave it alone.

A pumice-type sweater stone works on flat robust cloth and is a poor idea on anything delicate. A sticky lint roller lifts loose surface fluff but will not touch an anchored pill.

### The test standard nobody tells you about

Here is the genuinely useful thing to take away if you are choosing fabric.

Martindale does not measure pilling. The rub count everybody quotes — 25,000, 40,000, 100,000 — is an abrasion resistance figure, tested under BS EN ISO 12947. It tells you how long the fabric survives being rubbed. It says nothing whatsoever about whether it will bobble.

Pilling has its own standard: ISO 12945, which grades a fabric from 1 to 5, where 5 is no pilling and 1 is severe. Part 1 is the pilling box method, originally developed by ICI; part 2 is a modified Martindale method, and part 2 is the one usually quoted for upholstery. Confusingly it runs on the same machine as the abrasion test — but it is assessing how the surface looks, not when the cloth breaks down. A good upholstery fabric should be grade 4 to 5.

Most spec sheets carry it. Almost no customer asks for it, and a great many people have bought a 40,000-rub fabric assuming that covered everything, then been surprised. If bobbling would irritate you, ask for the pilling grade as well as the Martindale. Our chapter on choosing the right fabric covers how to read the rest of a spec sheet.

### When it is genuinely a fault

Worth complaining about if:

- Severe pilling appears within weeks rather than months.

- It is still producing new pills at the same rate after a year.

- The fabric was sold with a pilling grade of 4 or 5 and is plainly behaving like a 2.

- It is pilling in areas nobody touches, which suggests a problem with the cloth rather than with friction.

Not worth complaining about if it appeared in the first few months, on contact areas, on a soft blended fabric, and is slowing down. That is the cloth doing what that construction does, and no supplier will accept it as a defect — because it isn't one.

### The short version

Buy a fabric shaver, use it gently, and stop worrying. Most bobbling is a phase rather than a decline, and the fabric underneath is generally in perfectly good order.

And when you next choose a cloth, ask two numbers rather than one. The rub count tells you how long it lasts. The pilling grade tells you how it will look while it does.

### Common questions

#### Is pilling a fabric fault?

Usually not. Pilling is loose staple fibre migrating to the surface and tangling, which is a property of how the yarn was spun rather than evidence of misuse or a defect. It normally peaks in the first three to six months and then declines sharply. It is worth raising as a fault if severe pilling appears within weeks, if it is still producing new pills at the same rate after a year, or if the fabric was specified at pilling grade 4 to 5 and is clearly performing far worse.

#### How do you remove bobbles from a sofa?

With a battery fabric shaver, used with light pressure on a flat supported surface, in short overlapping passes, emptying the collector regularly and vacuuming afterwards. Do not pull pills off by hand, because they are anchored to fibres running back into the yarn and pulling removes cloth as well. Do not use a razor blade, and never use one on velvet, chenille or any pile fabric.

#### Does sofa pilling stop eventually?

On a decent fabric, yes. There is only a finite amount of loose fibre in the cloth, so once it has worked its way out and been shaved off, the surface stabilises. The worst of it is usually in the first three to six months. Pilling that continues at the same rate beyond a year suggests a yarn that is genuinely shedding, which is worth taking up with the supplier.

#### Which upholstery fabrics do not pill?

Filament-yarn fabrics, where the fibre runs continuously through the thread instead of being spun from short staple lengths — microfibre, most performance polyesters and solution-dyed acrylics. Leather and vinyl do not pill at all. The worst offenders are loosely spun staple blends such as poly-cotton and poly-wool, because the stronger fibre anchors pills formed by the weaker one rather than letting them break away.

## Wing-Back Armchair — Full Traditional Restoration — https://www.learntoupholster.com/wing-back-armchair

The wing-back is the major project of this book. It brings together every technique in Part Two on a single piece: full traditional springing, stitched-edge first-stuffing, complex inside-arm and wing geometry, careful pattern-matched cover work. A complete restoration takes us between 50 and 70 hours of workshop time and around £200–500 of materials. Customers are charged £2,200–2,900 for the labour, plus fabric. It is the project that pays the workshop’s bills, that we look forward to most, and that we charge a premium for justifiably.

This chapter walks through a complete wing-back restoration end-to-end, from the customer’s first phone call to the delivery van. It is the longest chapter in Part Three because the chair is the most complex; we have given it the room it deserves. Most of the techniques have been covered in Part Two; we’ll refer back rather than re-explain.

If you’ve worked through Chapters 7–17 carefully, you have all the technical background you need to follow this chapter. If you haven’t, this chapter will read as an overview rather than a manual; refer back as needed.

Don’t take a wing-back as your first major project. Do five [drop-ins](https://www.learntoupholster.com/drop-in-dining-seat) and three [stuffovers](https://www.learntoupholster.com/stuffover-dining-chair) first; do at least one [stool with deep buttoning](https://www.learntoupholster.com/stool-pouffe); only then commit to a wing-back. We’ve seen apprentices try to start here; the chair takes two months and the result is rarely satisfying.

### Wing-back anatomy

Wing-backs come in two main forms: the Georgian (c.1720–1810), with sloping wings and a low seat; and the Victorian (c.1850 onwards), with more vertical wings and a higher seat. Both share the same fundamental geometry: a tall back, two arms with vertical ‘wings’ rising from the arm-back junction up to almost the height of the cresting, and a deep seat with a stitched front edge. The wings provided draught protection in the unheated rooms of pre-central-heating houses; they remained on the chair as a design element long after the original purpose disappeared.

*Figure: Side-on view of a typical wing-back showing the named parts. The wing rises vertically from the inside-arm–back junction; it provides draught protection and is the chair’s signature design element.*

There are dozens of named wing-back variants — the Knole, the Howard, the Victoria & Albert — each with characteristic dimensions and trim. We’ll cover the general technique here; the variants are listed in Part Five ([Reference](https://www.learntoupholster.com/historical-style-guide)) with notes on what’s distinctive about each.

Total materials cost: £490–1,400 depending almost entirely on fabric choice.

#### Time estimate for the full restoration

| Strip and inspect | 4 hours |
|---|---|

| Webbing | 4 hours |
| Springing | 8–12 hours |

Allow a fortnight for a single wing-back if it’s the only thing on the bench; longer if other jobs are running in parallel.

We charge £80/hour for restoration work — that’s the two of us, Pat and me, on the bench, so effectively £40 per person-hour. A wing-back labour quote runs £2,200–2,900, with a price ceiling around £3,000 for fixed-price jobs. Plus materials and fabric. Customer expectation needs setting at the quote stage; many are surprised at the cost. (Full method in [pricing & quoting](https://www.learntoupholster.com/pricing-and-quoting).)

### The full build sequence

*Figure: Six stages of a wing-back restoration: frame, web, spring, stuff, calico, top cover. Each stage is its own days’ work; the chair changes character profoundly at each.*

#### Stage 1 Strip and inspect (4 hours)

Working through the chair in the order from [stripping the old work](https://www.learntoupholster.com/stripping-the-old-work). Top fabric off first (save the best pieces for cutting templates); calico off; second stuffing and felt off; scrim and stitched-edge first stuffing off; hessian off; springs and lashing off; webbing off. By the end the chair is a bare frame, and you know what you’re working with.

Wing-back inspection points: the eight joints of the main frame (back stiles to seat rails, arm rails to back stiles, arm rails to front legs); the wing structure (often a curved laminated piece, fragile); the cresting (often carved show-wood, expensive to repair); the front rail (heaviest tack damage usually). Photograph anything questionable; quote [frame repair](https://www.learntoupholster.com/frame-repair-and-joint-reinforcement) before committing to upholstery.

Save the original horsehair, every label, every brass castor, the original scrim if intact (use as a template for new). Bin the cover fabric, the felt and wadding (US: batting), the hessian (US: burlap). The horsehair is the most valuable thing the customer doesn’t know they have.

#### Stage 2 Frame repair if needed (variable)

Quote any frame work separately and get the customer’s sign-off before starting. Common wing-back frame issues: loose joints between back stiles and seat rails (re-glue with hide glue, see [frame repair](https://www.learntoupholster.com/frame-repair-and-joint-reinforcement)); split arm rails (splice in new section, joinery work); wing structure cracked or snapped (often the laminated wing piece needs full replacement, joinery work).

Don’t skip this step. A loose frame is what destroys the upholstery you’re about to build; the chair flexes at every sit and the new stitches break. Better to spend half a day fixing the frame than to redo the upholstery in two years.

Major frame work goes to our cabinet-maker; we don’t attempt it ourselves. The cabinet-maker turns wing-back frame repairs around in 2–3 weeks and charges £200–500 depending on the work. Quote separately to the customer.

#### Stages 3–4 Webbing and springing (12–16 hours)

Webbing and springing are exactly as [webbing](https://www.learntoupholster.com/webbing) and [traditional springing](https://www.learntoupholster.com/springing-traditional). The wing-back’s seat takes 9 springs in a 3 × 3 grid; the back takes 6 lighter springs in a 2 × 3 grid. The webbing layout matches the spring pattern (one webbing strand per row of springs, plus one more for support). 8-knot lashing on both seat and back; bridle ties everywhere.

The arms of a wing-back are usually not sprung — just stuffed over a hessian-covered timber frame. This makes the arms simpler to upholster than the seat or back, but they still need careful first stuffing and stitched edges to maintain shape over decades.

Some wing-backs (particularly Howard pieces) have spring-up backs — the back is constructed with coil springs just like the seat. Others have only the stuffing, no springs. Check what was there originally and reproduce it; don’t add springs that weren’t there.

#### Stage 5 First stuffing and stitched edges (16–20 hours)

The wing-back has three stitched-edge pads to build: the seat, the inside back, and each inside arm (plus the wings, which are typically smaller pads without stitched edges). All five pads need bridling, stuffing, scrim cover, blind stitch, top stitch — the full [stitched-edge technique](https://www.learntoupholster.com/stuffing-and-stitched-edges).

The seat pad is the largest and follows the standard build. Use about 2 kg of horsehair for the first stuffing, packed firmly to give a 20 mm proud rim along the front edge before stitching. Three rows of blind stitch + one row of top stitch.

The inside back follows the same technique on a larger vertical surface. Use about 1.5 kg of horsehair; the back’s stitched edges are along the top (cresting) and the two sides (where the back meets the wings). More awkward to stitch because you’re working vertically rather than down onto a flat seat; allow the extra time.

The inside arms each need about 0.6 kg of horsehair and a stitched edge along the inside-facing side (where the arm meets the seat) and along the top (where the wing rises). The arm scroll — the curved front of each arm — needs particular care to keep the curve consistent with the chair’s design.

This is where the bulk of the labour lives. Stitched-edge work on a wing-back is roughly 40% of the total project hours. Don’t rush it; the work shows in the chair’s lifetime more than any other stage.

Build the pads in this order: seat first, then inside arms, then inside back, then wings. The seat sets the proportions; the arms and back fit to the seat; the wings fit to the arms and back.

#### Stages 6–7 Calico and top cover (14–18 hours)

Once all the first-stuffing pads are formed, the second stuffing goes on (see [stuffing & stitched edges](https://www.learntoupholster.com/stuffing-and-stitched-edges)) and then calico (see [calico, wadding & top cover](https://www.learntoupholster.com/calico-wadding-and-top-cover)). For a wing-back, the calico is fitted as separate panels for each major surface — seat, inside back, two inside arms, two wings. Total of six calico panels.

Each calico panel is fitted, marked, and used as the pattern for the matching top-fabric panel. The top cover is then fitted in the standard order: inside back lining, inside arms, inside back, seat, wings, outside arms, outside back. Eight panels total on a wing-back, sometimes more for very ornate designs.

The wings deserve particular attention. The cover wraps the wing on three sides (front, back, top) and tacks off underneath at the inside-arm/wing junction. Pleat the cover at the outside corner of each wing; tack the underside; cover the join with gimp (see [trimming & finishing](https://www.learntoupholster.com/trimming-and-finishing)).

On a wing-back with velvet, plan the pile direction carefully: pile downward on inside back and seat front; pile front-to-back on seat top; pile downward on outside back. Mark every panel as you cut.

#### Tools for the job

- [Magnetic tack hammer](https://www.learntoupholster.com/go/amazon?q=upholstery+Magnetic+tack+hammer&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.amazon.co.uk%2Fdp%2FB00DS5HJ7Q%3Ftag%3D842699-21)
- [Webbing strainer (stretcher)](https://www.learntoupholster.com/go/amazon?q=upholstery+Webbing+strainer+%28stretcher%29&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.amazon.co.uk%2Fdp%2FB0GZNSHW66%3Ftag%3D842699-21)
- [Double-pointed stitching needles](https://www.learntoupholster.com/go/amazon?q=upholstery+needles+double+pointed&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.amazon.co.uk%2Fs%3Fk%3Dupholstery%2Bneedles%2Bdouble%2Bpointed%26tag%3D842699-21)
- [Curved spring needle](https://www.learntoupholster.com/go/amazon?q=upholstery+spring+needle+curved&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.amazon.co.uk%2Fs%3Fk%3Dupholstery%2Bspring%2Bneedle%2Bcurved%26tag%3D842699-21)

From the workshop

### The Howard chair we worked on for a month

A customer brought us an 1880s Howard & Sons wing-back in early 2017. Original springing intact, stitched edges still good after 130 years, frame solid, but the cover fabric was in fragments and the cresting had a major split that needed cabinet-maker work first.

We sent the frame out for repair (3 weeks; £400). When it came back we did a full traditional restoration retaining the original springs and most of the horsehair, with new first-stuffing only where the existing was compressed beyond recovery. The customer chose a wool-mohair fabric at £180/m; total fabric was £1,440. Labour was 64 hours across four weeks; we charged £1,600. Total bill £3,440. The customer was delighted; the chair was photographed for an interiors magazine; we got two more wing-back commissions off the back of it. (For the other side of that coin, read [the wing-back that wasn’t a Howard](https://www.learntoupholster.com/the-wing-back-that-wasnt-a-howard).)

Did you know

### Why wing-backs survive when other Victorian chairs don’t

Wing-backs from the Victorian period are over-represented in surviving Victorian furniture today. The reason is structural: the wing-back’s deep seat and tall back put the centre of gravity low and the chair is exceptionally stable. It rarely tips, rarely gets damaged in moves, and it sits comfortably enough that owners keep it in the drawing room rather than relegating it to a spare bedroom.

Other Victorian forms — the prie-dieu, the ‘ladies’ chair’, the smoking chair — have higher centres of gravity and were always more fragile. They survive in much smaller numbers. The wing-back’s longevity is partly the technique we cover in this chapter; partly its underlying physics.

Common mistakes

### Wing-back errors that catch beginners (and us) out

- Skipping the frame inspection — a loose-jointed wing-back will destroy your new upholstery. Inspect; repair; only then upholster.
- Wrong first stuffing volume — 2 kg in the seat, 1.5 kg in the back, 0.6 kg in each arm. Less and the chair feels under-built; more and the cover won’t fit.
- Stitching the back vertically — the inside back needs stitching while the chair lies on its back, not while it stands up. Working vertically you can’t get the stitches consistent. Tip the chair down.
- Mis-matching the wing to the arm — the wing rises from the inside-arm/back junction at a specific angle that’s part of the chair’s character. Reproduce the original angle; don’t ‘improve’ the design.
- Quoting too low — wing-backs are big-budget jobs. Customer expectation needs setting at the quote stage; if they baulk at £2,500 labour, the project isn’t for them — refer them to a foam-and-staple shop instead.
Wing-back restored, 60 hours of labour, customer delighted. The next project chapter is the wing-back’s larger sibling — the Chesterfield sofa — which adds deep buttoning (US: diamond tufting) across the inside back and arms, plus 22 pages of leather to handle.


---
By Shaun Greenwood, master upholsterer (AMUSF accredited). Part of The Working Upholsterer’s Bible, free at https://www.learntoupholster.com/

## Winning contract clients — https://www.learntoupholster.com/business/winning-contract-clients

### How do I get care home, hotel and commercial work?

Not by cold emailing them, on the evidence. We have sent a lot of approaches to care homes, hotels and facilities management firms and had almost no replies at all. The contract work we actually hold came three other ways: a formal approved-contractor process that took a year, a client who came to us, and one cold email that landed — and that one was a heritage property with antique furniture, not a chain. The pattern is that commercial buyers reply when nobody else can solve their problem, and ignore you when they already have a supplier.

### Start with the honest bit

Most advice about commercial upholstery work tells you to build a prospect list and start emailing. Care homes, hotels, restaurants, facilities management companies, property developers. It sounds like a plan, and it is what I did.

The reply rate was close to zero.

Not one polite no thank you from most of them. Nothing at all. And the emails were not bad — they were short, specific, and from an AMUSF-accredited workshop with thirty years behind it.

That is worth saying plainly, because if you are sitting looking at a spreadsheet of unanswered approaches and assuming you are doing it wrong, you probably are not. The tactic is weak, not you.

### Why they do not reply

Once you look at it from their side it stops being mysterious.

**They already have someone.** Care homes and hotel groups of any size have facilities management arrangements in place. Soft furnishings sit inside a contract that was signed long before your email arrived, and nobody in the building has the authority or the appetite to unpick it.

**They replace, they do not repair.** This is the big one. Commercial furniture is bought as a capital item on a replacement cycle. When the chairs in the lounge look tired, the default is a purchase order for new chairs, not a search for an upholsterer. Reupholstery is not a line in the budget because nobody has ever put it there.

**The person who opens the email cannot buy anything.** Your message lands with a receptionist, a duty manager, or a generic inbox. The person who could actually authorise the spend is two steps away and never sees it.

**You are solving a problem they have not noticed yet.** A worn chair is not urgent. It becomes urgent when a fire risk assessment flags it, when a refurbishment is planned, or when something breaks. Your email almost never arrives on that day.

### What actually worked

Three routes, and none of them was cold email at scale.

#### 1. Approved contractor status

The holiday park work came through a formal approved-contractor process with a large operator. Insurance at their required level, fire compliance evidence, method statements, risk assessments. It took a year.

That is slow, but it is the most reliable route there is, because at the end of it you are on a list that gets consulted rather than in an inbox that gets deleted. Once you are on it, the work is steady and repeating. There is more on how that market actually operates in [caravan and holiday park work](https://www.learntoupholster.com/business/caravan-and-holiday-park-work).

#### 2. They came to us

The hotel work arrived through an investment group approaching the workshop, not the other way round. That happens when you are visible and credible — a portfolio, an accreditation, a website, work photographed properly — and it happens on their timetable, not yours.

You cannot force it. You can make sure that when somebody does go looking, there is something to find.

#### 3. One cold email out of many

And then there is the one that landed, which is the interesting one.

### The castle

A castle in the UK, owned by a large company and let out as a venue. Antique furniture that had been in the building for decades: a two-seat wing settee and two old armchairs.

They needed fitted loose covers. Because of the layout of the building and the nature of the pieces, the furniture was not going anywhere — so the work started with a site visit, templating and measuring up in situ, then making the covers to those templates. They supplied the cloth themselves; we did the making and fitting.

Now ask why that enquiry got a reply when a hundred care homes did not.

**Because nobody else could solve it.** You cannot buy a replacement for a settee that has been in a castle for eighty years. You cannot ring a contract furniture supplier and order one. The default option that kills every other commercial approach — *just buy new* — simply was not available.

That is the whole lesson, and it took a year of unanswered emails to see it.

### What that tells you about who to approach

Stop emailing organisations. Start emailing problems.

The commercial clients who reply are the ones holding furniture that cannot be replaced, or cannot easily be:

- Heritage properties, castles, halls and historic houses let as venues

- Listed buildings where the interiors are part of what is being preserved

- Private estates and family seats

- Members' clubs, livery halls, masonic halls, golf clubs with old fixed seating

- Theatres and cinemas with original seating

- Universities and schools with panelled rooms and period furniture

- Antique dealers and auction houses supplying the trade

- Boutique hotels that bought character furniture deliberately

- Churches and cathedrals



Compare that list with care homes and budget hotel chains. The difference is not size or budget. It is whether *buy new* is an option. Where it is, you will not hear back. Where it is not, you are the only answer.

**One good approach to a heritage property is worth fifty to a care home group.**

### Approach the right person, and be specific

The other thing that separates a reply from silence is who reads it and what it says.

For a heritage venue, the person you want is the house manager, the estates manager, the curator or the conservation officer — not a generic enquiries address. For a private company operating a venue, it is whoever holds the building rather than whoever handles bookings.

And say something specific. Not "we offer commercial upholstery services", which is indistinguishable from every other email they get. Something closer to:

> "I noticed you have period seating in the main hall. If any of it needs recovering, I work on antique frames and can make fitted loose covers on site where furniture cannot be moved. AMUSF accredited, thirty years, £5m public liability."

That names the problem, names the constraint they are worried about — *the furniture cannot leave the building* — and answers the insurance question before they ask it.

### The fire question is different, and you must raise it

Commercial premises are not domestic, and the specification changes.

Where furniture is in a public building, **BS 7176** sets hazard categories by environment, and most public venues sit at medium hazard, meaning crib 5. Fillings separately have to satisfy the Furniture and Furnishings (Fire) (Safety) Regulations 1988 as amended.

Heritage work sits in a genuinely awkward spot. Goods made before 1950 are excluded from the 1988 Regulations, which is why antique restoration does not force period pieces into modern materials. But that exclusion is about the furniture, and BS 7176 is about the building. An antique settee in a public venue can therefore be both legitimately exempt and sitting in a room whose fire risk assessment expects a hazard category.

There is no single right answer to that, and it is not your call to make alone. **Get the requirement in writing from whoever is responsible for the building**, before you cut anything, and put their answer on the job sheet. If they supply the cloth, as the castle did, get the fire evidence for it at the same time — see [customer's own fabric](https://www.learntoupholster.com/business/customer-supplied-fabric).

The [fire regulations checker](https://www.learntoupholster.com/fire-safety-checker) walks through both regimes if you need to work out where a specific job sits.

### What I would do differently

Looking back at a year of it:

1. **Far fewer approaches, far better targeted.** Ten letters to heritage properties beats two hundred emails to care homes.

2. **Write to a named person**, and post it. A letter to the house manager of a historic property is unusual enough to get read. An email is not.

3. **Lead with the constraint you solve** — on-site work, furniture that cannot be moved, antique frames, fitted loose covers. Not with a list of services.

4. **Chase the approved contractor lists early**, because they take a year and the clock only starts when you apply.

5. **Photograph everything**, because the castle job is now the thing that wins the next one.



### The honest summary

I hold contract work. It is a real and useful part of the business, and the holiday park side genuinely smooths out the year.

Almost none of it came from cold emailing commercial clients, and I would not put much more time into that. The routes that worked were a slow formal application, being findable when somebody went looking, and one well-aimed approach to a place with a problem nobody else could fix.

If you take one thing from this: commercial buyers do not respond to availability. They respond to being stuck.
